subtopic: TABLING OF STATEMENT ON ENLARGEMENT OF EUROPEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my recent talks with English and European representatives responsible for the negotiations, I highlighted four main themes:
1.	Our concerns about the negative effects of E.E.C. enlargement on Canada's access to markets and on the framework and patterns of world trade.
2.	Our conviction that in some instances mutuality of interests exists between Canada and Britain and the E.E.C., should bring about agreements beneficial to all.
3.	Our intention to bring into play at an appropriate stage the contractual rights and obligations, under bilateral arrangements and under the GATT, which would be affected by E.E.C. enlargement.
4.	Our views as to the importance of developing new initiatives for freeing of trade during the period of European negotiations.
In discussing the direct impact E.E.C. enlargement would have on Canadian trade, I drew a statistical picture of the changes in access terms which our exports to Britain would face if that country adopted the E.E.C. Common External Tariff and the Common Agricultural Policy unchanged.
It was essential for all negotiating countries to know that almost 70 per cent of our exports to Britain would be adversely affected if this took place.
As regards the more general implications, I emphasized the danger of polarization of world trade into inwardlooking rival blocks.
I urged that the European Community use its influence to facilitate and encourage continued expansion of trade on a world-wide basis and not only within its own grouping of member and associated countries. If E.E.C. enlargement mainly has the effect of limiting and diverting trade from third countries, the Community itself would lose over the longer run in terms of consumer and producer costs. Moreover, outside suppliers could not remain indifferent to the loss of important traditional markets for their goods in the E.E.C. and in the countries associated with it.
Britain has already told the E.E.C. that it is prepared in principle to accept the Common External Tariff and the Common Agricultural Policy.
Certain special arrangements which Britain is seeking in its own interest could help some of our exports. Nine of the twelve industrial materials for which Britain has requested special arrangements are of interest to Canada. Needless to say, there will also be a transitional period for the necessary adjustments.
Mr. Speaker, on the basis of my discussions with European leaders, I can say that Britain and the E.E.C. are prepared to maintain a two-way flow of views and information with Canada throughout the negotiations. They are also willing to explore with us areas where their interests may, to some extent, coincide with our own.
It would be misleading for me to suggest, however, that there is a prospect for a major accommodation of Canadian trade interests in the short term. We must assume that, if the negotiations succeed, Canadian exports to Britain will eventually be subject to a Common External Tariff and a Common Agricultural Policy.
Canada would be less concerned, I told my interlocutors, if, apart from "elargissement" and "approfondissement , they started planning for "mondialisation"_____or
adaptation of the results of enlargement to the interests

December 1, 1970
European Trade
of freer world trade. This could take place during the negotiations or before the end of the transitional period.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)

In both Brussels and London I found the tendency to argue that the Canadians were exaggerating the negative impact of EEC enlargement on their trade and minimizing the importance of the growth that would follow enlargement in Europe, particularly in terms of import needs.
We were repeatedly assured by all that the policy of the EEC-and perhaps even more so of an enlarged
EEC____would be responsible and outward looking. I said
Canadians sincerely hoped that events would bear out these assertions.
What will be the Canadian attitude in the months and years to come? We shall continue to seek areas of mutuality of interests. We shall continue to urge the EEC and the applicant countries, when they are weighing the merits of alternative solutions, to include in the balance the interests of third countries and the future of the world trading community.
As the negotiations in Europe proceed, we shall be considering how our important contractual rights and obligations can be put into play most effectively. We shall also be reviewing the implications of EEC enlargement for Britain's preferential access to the Canadian market.
In the meantime, we shall use our influence in the GATT to maintain the momentum of trade liberalization efforts and press in particular for a major round of negotiations before the results of the enlargement negotiations are put into effect. We shall continue to urge the United States to provide, with the EEC and other major world traders, the leadership and support which is essential if these efforts are to succeed.
We shall have no illusions, however, that we can safely leave the protection of Canadians interests to others. As a major trading partner of Britain and a significant market for the EEC and the applicant countries, Canada is not Without bargaining power.
It will continue to be a key objective of Canadian policy to intensify our trading relations with Europe as a whole As illustrated in my tabled statement, a greater emphasis is being given to this area over a wide range of the programs of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The public and private sectors in Canada will have to work closely together in order to minimize the effects of EEC enlargement on our trade and to maximize its positive elements. I know that we can count on all sectors of Canadian industry, and I can assure them and the House that the government will do its part.
Hon Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
Mr Speaker, I am glad to see that the government has at last apparently decided to take some interest in the negotiations that are going on for the expansion of the
IMr. Pepin.)
European Economic Community. This first indication of concern for developments in an area of major trading importance for Canada has been rather late in coming. And, unlike what we are told happens in the kingdom of heaven, there is no guarantee here that a late conversion means salvation.
I have been suggesting for some time that Canada should move quickly to make sure that her interests are not ignored when, as now seems likely, Britain and a number of other European countries enter the Common Market. Once that happens, this will be the largest trading bloc in the world, and let us not forget that. I have suggested, too, that the longer Canada waited to show its concern the harder it would be for us to have any impact. Hopefully, we have not waited too long, but from the minister's statement it is clear that beyond some polite assurances that things will not be too bad, he has come home emptyhanded. This is bad news for Canadian exporters, and particularly so for our fanners who have been selling millions of dollars worth of produce a year on the British market, and who must now contemplate competing in the protected Common Market.
I must ask if we are not faced here with some chickens coming home to roost? For the last couple of years, the government has followed a policy of retrenchment in foreign affairs. We have indicated a lack of interest in the affairs of Britain and the Commonwealth. We have partially withdrawn from participation in NATO and we have not even bothered for almost a year-until yesterday in fact-to have an ambassador in Brussels which is where the action is as far as the Common Market is concerned.
As a result, it is not really surprising, when one visits London and Brussels, as I did last summer, to find that the general feeling seems to be that Canada just is not concerned about the problems of Europe. The minister himself said he noted a tendency among people to whom he spoke to downgrade the effects of these developments upon Canada. It is surprising, Sir, that it should be late fall when a Canadian minister discovers this on behalf of the government of Canada. If that is the case, the obvious response is for Europe to lose interest in us. Why should it worry about our interests in Europe if we do not show any concern ourselves?

maintopic: ROUTINE PROCEEDINGS

speechtext:
There is no question about the general feeling in official circles in Britain and western Europe that Canada has lost interest in developing relations with Europe. The only concern we have shown is to complain about the Common Market allegedly discriminating against us on a few occasions. To this the Common Market people shoot back that we have indulged in exactly the same practices, only worse. I see an article in the Gazette today headlined, "Common Market Officials Laugh at Canada's Complaints." This is a measure of the loss of Canadian popularity and influence that has been going on for the last few years. This is why I charge that the government has been negligent. This is why I find so intriguing the assertion on page 7 of the minister's state-
December 1, 1970

ment that Canada is not without bargaining power. That is wonderful to hear, but instead of talking about it why have we not been using this bargaining power? Why has it not done any good yet? Why are we not using it right now? I realize that it is very comforting for a government to talk about power rather than use it, but in this situation, if such power does exist, we had better use it.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
Whatever our present bargaining situation may be, the minister's statement tells us clearly that the Canadian export economy is approaching dangerous times in relation to Europe. At the very least, I should have thought that this would force the government to take a serious look at our trading policies. But there is no sign of this. Instead, the minister merely offers us reassurances of good will that are even vaguer than the ones he received in Europe.
Does this mean that the present government has now reconciled itself to the fact that this country is simply going to slip unyielding into the embrace of North American continentalism? If so, it should tell the Canadian people that this is the case. If not, then we should have some indication that the government is seriously looking at the choices before us and at least trying to come up with alternative policies. This country must maintain and develop healthy trade patterns. Vague reassurances of the sort the minister has given us are not enough.

maintopic: ROUTINE PROCEEDINGS

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a most serious statement that has been put before us today and the implications for Canada are pretty grim unless something is done about them. I am sure that the minister was reflecting the opinion of all Canadians when he expressed the hope that world protectionism would not increase and that there would be the entry of Canada and other countries into the European Common Market. Nevertheless, we have to be realistic about what is happening and not put our heads in the sand in face of the present situation. We have to realize that much of the polarization of trade and the formation of blocs is a direct reaction to the international corporations and to the policies of the United States government.
The European Economic Community, unlike Canada, is very jealous of its sovereignty and is very much concerned about what is going to happen to Europe in the face of international corporations and their operations round the world. Europe is moving to do something about it. Their answer is to set up viable industry in Europe capable of competing on equal terms with the international corporations, sometimes using the international corporation as a start.
One of the worries that France had regarding Britain's entry into the Common Market was that Britain would serve as a stalking horse for the United States, that Britain, under the conditions she was advocating at that time, would influence American entry into the Common Market. It appears that assurances have now been given to the members of the Common Market that this is not
European Trade
the case and that Britain's entry is now just a matter of time. In his book "The American Challenge" Servan-Schreiber pointed out the difficulty facing Europe and the necessity of challenging the attempt of the United States to dominate the world through its commercial practices and international corporations.
The Leader of the Opposition used the phrase, "the chickens are coming home to roost". This is very true. When we look at our behaviour toward Great Britain and the way the trade pattern developed between Canada and Great Britain we must blame ourselves for the fact that year after year there was a great imbalance of trade m our favour. Over and over again spokesmen from England came to Canada and said it could not go on this way. They pointed out that Britain was no longer in a position to keep buying the goods that Canada had to offer when Canada was not buying from them.
When the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert was leader of the Conservative party, as part of his program he made an attempt to divert trade and increase Canada s imports from Great Britain. For one reason or another that attempt never came off; whether it was frustrated by the extent of United States ownership in Canada I do not know. The British people could not be expected to accept unlimited one-way trade and as a result they are not now terribly concerned with either the Commonwealth or future relationships with Canada. This should not be too surprising, nor come as a shock to us.
Again, if we want to engage in international trade we shall have to provide some assurance to the other nations of the world we trade with that we are not going to be part of the American empire and that the Americans will not obtain entry to the Common Market through us. If we are to trade in some kind of independent fashion with other nations we shall have to assert our own sovereignty and independence and make it appear that we mean to do so and that we do not intend to remain in the satellite position we now occupy.
I sympathize with the problems of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) I think he win have to continue acting along the lines he has blocked out m his statement. We should do everything possible to indicate to the Europeans that it is our desire to trade with them, and we should see what sort of arrangements can be worked out. Perhaps there could even be some kind of associate status for us in the Common Market so that our entry would not be barred. If we are unsuccessful in our attempts, we shall be faced with two horrendous choices, continentalism or isolation from world trade, or a third choice which may be what the minister referred to when he said we have some bargaining power. We are a very fortunate nation.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) for having circulated a copy of the French version of the statement he made today in the House.
On behalf of my colleagues and in my own name, I am pleased to congratulate the minister for the steps taken by the government with a view to allowing Canada to keep up, if not to increase, its import and export trade with the European Economic Community countries.

I repeat, the time has come for us to become a sort of link or even get in the van to promote world-wide trade, no matter with what country we make exchanges. However we must ensure that the prices paid by countries for various products on world markets will not be detrimental to the Canadian market owing to higher production cost in Canada with regard to other countries.
Therefore, I invite the government to pursue those efforts and this kind of mediation with the world powers in order to extend trade to world dimensions and, if possible, to find greater markets.

BAY OF FUNDY TIDES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to ask leave of the House to make a motion under Standing Order 43 requesting that immediate action be taken by the government to reconsider the decision rendered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with regard to the harnessing of the Bay of Fundy tides from a power point of view on November 24, 1970, when he stated, "There is no provision for reconsidering this matter at this time". I make this motion in light of the fact that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) told the House on May 29, 1970, that he would "see whether a valid review could be undertaken".
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
When the Atlantic Tidal Power Programming Board presented its findings to the federal government, it stated that interest rates were the basic reason for not proceeding with the project at the present time. After that report was made public an International Conference on the Utilization of Tidal Power was held at Halifax from May 24 to May 29, with the consensus of that conference favouring an early start on the harnessing of the tides. Interest rates have dropped and are continuing to drop. Power demand is on the increase in both Canada and the United States. An immediate market would be available for the power, once produced.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: BAY OF FUNDY TIDES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext: Order, please. I have to interrupt the hon. member. He knows he cannot make a speech at this time. maintopic: BAY OF FUNDY TIDES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
I therefore move:
That this House urges the government to take immediate steps to reconsider the report of the Atlantic Tidal Power Programming Board, coupled with the reports of the International Conference on the Utilization of Tidal Power, and-in view of falling interest rates and chronic and rising unemployment in the Maritime provinces, and substantial demand for the power that could be produced, with a view to harnessing the tides of the Bay of Fundy for power purposes at the earliest date possible.

speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-177, respecting co-operation associations, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

maintopic: CANADA CO-OPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS BILL INCORPORATION. ARTICLES OF ASSOCIATION, SHARE STRUCTURE, GENERAL POWERS AND DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
That Bill C-177, An Act respecting co-operative associations, be amended by deleting all the words after the word "and" in line 21 of paragraph (d) of clause 68, and substituting therefor the following:
'the directors shall also appoint all other officers thereof.'
He said: Mr. Speaker, may I take a moment to explain, briefly, the purpose of the amendment. Its purpose is to leave no doubt that only the board of directors of any co-operative shall appoint an officer of that co-operative. We have had some discussion about this matter with senior people from the national co-operative movement. After discussing the point when the bill was before the committee, I moved an amendment which appeared not to be suitable. I therefore withdrew it so that the matter might be discussed further, with the hope that we could bring in another amendment during the present stage of the bill.
I have discussed this matter with other people who are concerned about this legislation. As the bill presently reads, it is possible for the president or vice president of a co-operative, who have been appointed by the board of directors, to appoint other officers. Actually, from my reading of the pertinent paragraph, it appears that even if the board of directors does not appoint certain officers, those officers may be appointed by the president, vice president or other officers and the act would not be thereby violated. I do not think that is the intention of this law. Admittedly, such an event is unlikely, but that it should be at all possible I believe is contrary to the common practice and wishes of the co-operative movement.
My second point is this: It seems that an officer of the co-operative movement who has not been elected can, as the language of the bill now stands, appoint another officer, without the authority of the directors of the cooperative concerned so to do. I invite hon. members to look at subparagraph (k) on page 3 of the bill, where "officer" is defined. There an officer is defined, among other things, as the president, vice-president, secretary, treasurer, comptroller, general manager, managing director or any other individual who performs the functions of an officer. The senior management personnel are pretty well covered by the definition and they are not all elected officials. These men are defined as officers. According to the wording of the bill, an officer who has not been elected but who has been perhaps appointed by the board may appoint another officer without asking authority of the board of directors. For example, as I see it, a general manager who has been appointed by the board of directors, and who is an officer according to the definition of the bill, may in turn appoint another officer, let us say
December 1, 1970

the comptroller. That comptroller would be an officer who had been appointed without the authority of the board of directors.
I admit that this is not likely to happen in any well organized and well operated co-operative, but I think that we have a dangerous loophole in the law. No matter how intelligently the law is interpreted, it is open for officers of the co-operative, as defined in the bill, to appoint other officers without first seeking the authority of the elected membership of the co-operative, namely the board of directors. There is a danger that the tail could wag the dog; and since the co-operative movement has been waiting over 60 years for this legislation, that is a danger we ought to avoid. For that reason, I think the amendment is proper. If adopted, I submit that the wording of the pertinent part of the bill would be improved. I hope the minister and the House will see fit to adopt it.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words for the record to explain what happened during the committee proceedings. A number of amendments were made to Bill C-177 respecting co-operative associations. I wish to comment on them briefly.
During second reading of this bill on November 2, representatives of all parties in this House expressed their agreement with the principle of the bill, although some reservations were expressed in connection with a number of specific provisions. As a matter of fact, after consultations with the co-operative movement and discussion in committee on November 25, we accepted a few
Canada Co-operative Associations Bill amendments which do not change in any way the philosophy of the bill or its structure. I commend the bill to all hon. members and to the co-operative movement of Canada.
The Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, to which Bill C-177 was referred, heard from the cooperative movement which was represented by Mr. W. B. Melvin, president of the Co-operative Union of Canada, and his associates, and Mr. Martin Leger, president of Le Conseil Canadien de Co-operation, both of whom expressed the approval and support of their organizations for Bill C-177. I wish to read into the record a short statement made by Mr. Melvin before the committee:
As I am sure you will appreciate, the introduction of Bill C-177 entitled "Canada Co-operative Associations Act" is an event of great significance for the co-operative sector of the Canadian economy. Indeed, co-operators have awaited this legislation for something over 60 years. Governments have come and gone in long succession since the year 1908 to the point where we almost doubted that it could happen.
I find some satisfaction and honour in the fact that I am the minister who, after approximately 63 years, is able to introduce this legislation which has received the approval of all parties. I wish to mention briefly the amendments that were made.
The original words in clause 5 of the bill required any co-operative seeking a national charter to have an office or place of business in each province. These words were replaced by the words "in more than one province". It appeared to some members of the committee that the original text of the bill could be a little too cumbersome and rigid if it received a strict interpretation. Co-operative associations would have been required to have a fixed place of business in each province where they carry on their business. The effects of the amendment is to remove any possible doubts. As a result, it will be sufficient for a co-operative to have a fixed place of business in more than one province. This amendment clarifies the scope of application of the bill and we are pleased to accept it.
Perhaps the most important amendment which was made by the committee concerns the repayment to withdrawing members of loans made to an association. This amendment differentiates the time of repayment depending on whether it is a demand loan or a term loan. It clarifies the provisions of the bill as to the terms of repayment.
The last amendment, asked for by the co-operative movement, has the effect of extending in clause 101 the grounds upon which an inspection or investigation could be carried out. The purpose of the amendment is to permit an inspection or investigation to be carried out for reasons in addition to those specified in the bill, namely that there is reason to believe an association has ceased to carry on its undertaking on a co-operative basis. With the amendments made in committee, the bill has the support of all members of the committee and of the co-operative movement across Canada.
I wish to express my thanks to members of the committee for the expeditious way that they dealt with this bill. I think that those who were somewhat critical of the

December 1, 1970
Canada Co-operative Associations Bill decision to send the bill to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs will now see the wisdom of that decision in the light of the very excellent way the chairman and members of the committee from all parties dealt with the bill.
I also want to express my appreciation to members of the co-operative movement of Canada with whom my officials consulted over the last 18 months when drawing this bill. I also express my appreciation to the officials of the various provincial co-operative branches with whom my officials had the honour and privilege of meeting on a number of occasions. We were able to learn from these provincial officials with regard to the proper drafting of a national co-operatives act.
The fact that this bill has received widespread support in this House, received speedy and expeditious approval of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and received the uncritical support of the co-operative movement, is indicative of the value of the consultative process that occurred during the course of preparing this bill when meeting provincial officials and members of the co-operative associations. As a result, the government is able to place before Parliament a bill that has the overwhelming approval which this bill has received.
As I said on second reading, Mr. Speaker, the first co-operative bill was introduced and passed in this House in 1908. It was then defeated in the other place. Since that time those interested in the co-operative movement have been looking forward to an act permitting them to incorporate on a national basis. This bill provides the machinery by which co-operatives that organize and operate in more than one province can come to the federal government for a federal charter. That is a very important step to the co-operative movement. I am proud that I, as the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, am the one entitled to pilot this bill through the House.

maintopic: CANADA CO-OPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS BILL INCORPORATION. ARTICLES OF ASSOCIATION, SHARE STRUCTURE, GENERAL POWERS AND DUTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words in support of the final disposition of this bill in this House of Commons. It is a great moment to have this legislation before us, and it was perhaps the greatest moment in the recent history of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. There was some doubt about whether our committee would be able to stand up to the presence of such awesome legislation. We did our best to accept the challenge.
Perhaps our greatest moment in modern times was when the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) appeared before the committee with great humility and suggested that the present legislation was the result of a force far stronger than any royal commission. When I pressed to find what was greater than the force of a royal commission, I found out it was the committee headed by the minister a number of years ago when he was a humble back bencher. The humility on the face of the minister when he made that pronouncement will be cherished by me throughout this session.
The minister deserves his moment of grandeur. As pointed out by the member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), it has been many years since legislation of this type was attempted in Parliament. The last attempt failed. Now that we have experienced the easy disposition of this bill in our chamber, it seems strange that there was such difficulty before. When speaking in this debate on November 2, as recorded at page 791 of Hansard, the hon. member for St. John's East said and I quote:
A bill of a similar nature was before Parliament in 1908 but was defeated by the other place for reasons which it would probably not be useful to go into at this particular time.
The reason the other place was ungentle with a measure of this sort in 1908 is an interesting historical fact, but we live in rapidly changing times. Perhaps this bill is the result of what Marshall McLuhan has called the development of the global village concept. The pace of communications has forced us into adopting this measure so that co-operatives which deal interprovincially will have a greater scope for their work. This is really the purpose of the bill.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
It is a long bilL I think it is probably longer than the latest edition of the New Testament, as I somewhat irreverently remarked when it was being considered in committee. It is a long measure but its legal effect is simply to give recognition to the fact that co-operatives which operate across provincial boundaries have been established in Canada. For example, a co-operative established in Regina may operate in both Alberta and Manitoba, or a co-operative established in Moncton may deal with Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and have some connection with Newfoundland. In short, the bill gives legal blessing to something which is a fact in Canada today. As a Member of Parliament coming from Nova Scotia where we have done great work in the co-operative field-we were, in fact, the pioneers, as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) has been good enough to say-it gives me special pleasure to support this legislation enthusiastically. Once again, I cannot for the life of me imagine why, 62 years ago, there should have been any difficulty placed in the way of the co-operative movement by one of the chambers of this place.
May I make a few brief points in closing, Mr. Speaker? I think the bill has been well put together. It is a classic example of what we can do with legislation as a Parliament if due regard is paid to the needs of those who are directly concerned, if due regard is paid by the minister to getting the nitty-gritty of the legislation out of the way before it is presented either to the House or to a committee of Parliament. This is what the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has done. He has taken this measure, he has vetted it with the people most directly affected; it has been fine tooth-combed probably a half dozen times. All this effort brought its reward. The bill had good going in the committee, but not tough going, because we recognized what had been done by the minister and his officials before they brought it before us. Then, of course, hon. members on both sides of the House had accepted the principles of the measure. This is a

December 1, 1970

good example of what can be done when legislation is tackled in this way, and accordingly we support it without reservation.

maintopic: BUFFALO AND FORT ERIE PUBLIC BRIDGE COMPANY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING BORROWING POWER AND TERMINATION OF JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Buffalo and Fort Erie Bridge Authority which operates an international bridge known as the Peace Bridge between Buffalo, New York, and Fort Erie, Ontario, was incorporated pursuant to a

December 1, 1970
Buffalo and Fort Erie Bridge Act statute passed in 1933 by the legislature of the State of New York. Property and assets of the Bridge Authority in Canada, however, are acquired, held and managed pursuant to an act of Parliament entitled, "An Act respecting the Buffalo and Fort Erie Public Bridge Company" passed in 1934 and amended for the first time in 1957, and which this bill proposes again to amend.
The Authority consists of 10 members, five of whom are citizens of the United States and five of whom are Canadian citizens appointed by Governor in Council. The position of Chairman of the Authority alternates annually between Canadian and United States appointees.
The bill presently before the House is intended to amend two provisions of the existing legislation. The first amendment is in respect of the limit of the Authority's borrowing power which presently stands at $4 million. This will be increased to $15 million. The second amendment is in respect of the date on which the rights, powers and jurisdiction of the Bridge Authority are to be terminated and the property held by it in Canada to become the property of Her Majesty.
Whereas the existing statute stipulates that the reversionary date is July 1, 1992, or the date on which outstanding bonds are redeemed, whichever is the latter, the proposed bill would substitute July 1, 2020 in lieu of July 1, 1992. The Bridge Authority has been reviewing its long-range plans and anticipates the need to widen the present bridge to accommodate additional traffic. To this end, the Authority will have to borrow additional funds to finance improvements in capital facilities. The provisions of the present bill are designed to put the Authority in a position to proceed with this project.
An act was passed May 13, 1970 by the legislature of the State of New York incorporating amendments corresponding to those proposed in the present bill.

maintopic: BUFFALO AND FORT ERIE PUBLIC BRIDGE COMPANY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING BORROWING POWER AND TERMINATION OF JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to say that we on this side of the House are in accord with the amendments which have been presented here. This is a very short bill with very little detail in it. There is very little to understand about it and, therefore, the bill should take very little time to pass through this House. As a matter of fact, it would seem to me to be quite in order not to send the bill to the committee for study but to handle it in the Committee of the Whole House, thereby accelerating the passage of the legislation. I trust that the government might find some means whereby this can be accomplished.
There are some general comments I should perhaps make on the Peace Bridge, as it is commonly known and as referred to by the hon. member who introduced the amendment. It serves the people of western New York state and southern Ontario. It is the terminus of the Queen Elizabeth Way and also No. 3 provincial highway across southern Ontario. This bridge provides a means for United States tourists to visit tourist areas along our north shore. I was pleased to hear during the introduction of these amendments that the purpose is to improve the bridge and widen it. This is long overdue because, as I have pointed out, it serves this part of southern Ontario

and western New York State where the traffic has doubled or tripled since its erection. The widening of it is therefore long overdue.
The bridge serves the north shore of Lake Erie where there are several resort areas to which United States tourists are attracted. This is the easiest access route. I have in mind such areas as Woodlawn Park, Peacock Point, Port Dover, Turkey Point and Point Rowan.

maintopic: BUFFALO AND FORT ERIE PUBLIC BRIDGE COMPANY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING BORROWING POWER AND TERMINATION OF JURISDICTION
speechtext: Hurray for Turkey Point.

maintopic: BUFFALO AND FORT ERIE PUBLIC BRIDGE COMPANY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING BORROWING POWER AND TERMINATION OF JURISDICTION
speechtext:
The hon. member says, "Hurray for Turkey Point". I agree with him and I invite all hon. members to visit these lovely resort areas on Lake Erie. Despite all the adverse publicity about Lake Erie being a dead lake and a cesspool of North America, this is just not true of the north shore. The currents in the lake generally run along the south shore where the major pollution exists. Anyone who had a look at Lake Erie from a low flying light aircraft could easily see the difference in the colours between the north and south shores.
So, I want to say here and now that the resort areas on the north shore of Lake Erie are excellent places to spend a vacation and many United States people cross the Peace Bridge to visit this lovely part of Canada. This route is also of benefit to the people in this part of the United States in that they find the bridge route to No. 3 highway the shortest route between Buffalo and Detroit. This saves them detouring around the south of Lake Erie to get to their destination.
As I said at the beginning, we approve of this measure and feel we should not spend a lot of time in passing it. The purpose is quite clear and I am sure there is no skulduggery involved here as was intimated in respect of another bridge, namely at Port Huron. We on this side, therefore, suggest rapid passage and perhaps it can be handled by the Committee of the Whole.

maintopic: BUFFALO AND FORT ERIE PUBLIC BRIDGE COMPANY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING BORROWING POWER AND TERMINATION OF JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few remarks to make at the second reading stage. At the outset, I am in agreement with the suggestion of the previous speaker. I see no reason why we cannot deal with this bill in the Committee of the Whole without sending it to the standing committee. However, 1 leave that to the discretion of the Parliamentary Secretary and his colleagues.
In looking over the history of this company, and bridge legislation, in general which has been dealt with over the years, a number of questions come to mind. Perhaps these could be held until we get to the committee stage, but I note that in 1923, again in 1934 and 1957, there were amendments to the provision in respect of reversion of the property to the governments of Canada and the United States. We have continued to extend the date for this reversion. In 1957, the date was extended to 1992 and it is to be extended to 2020. I suppose that is far enough ahead to make sure that none of us are here when that date arrives. I wonder what the purpose is of having that provision in the bill. If it is a good idea to

December 1, 1970
have a public company operate the bridge, why worry about the reversion clause. Perhaps the United States is afraid the Parliamentary Secretary might saw the bridge in half and take our part home. I do not see the necessity for this clause unless we really intend that those parts of the bridge lying on either side of the international boundary become the property of the governments and people of our two respective nations. Personally, I would like to see that happen.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I do not see any point in having a separate company operate a public thoroughfare such as this bridge. I do not understand why this could not be done very shortly. From a reading of the debate of 1957, it would seem that had the act not been amended then the bonds would have been paid off by 1962 and the respective halves of the bridge would have reverted to the government of Canada and the government of the United States. I do not know why that was not allowed to happen. I do not doubt that originally the local people felt a need for the bridge and, therefore, formed a private company. During the period from 1923 to 1927, a Canadian counterpart company was formed and laws were enacted in the United States and in Canada. This situation has existed ever since. I would appreciate having more information from the Parliamentary Secretary when we deal with the bill at the committee stage, or perhaps he or one of his colleagues would give further answers now.
I appreciate the desire to increase the borrowing power of the company from $4 million to $15 million because of the necessity to widen the bridge, but I do not understand why these funds could not come from the public treasury of the two respective countries rather than as a result of issuing bonds and paying interest for many years. If it is necessary to have bonds, then I do not understand why the governments of Canada and the United States could not buy up 50 per cent of the bonds each and collect the interest themselves, as is the case in respect of CNR bonds. This would make more sense than adding an additional cost to the users of the bridge.
Back in 1923 or 1925, the amalgamation of the two companies was envisaged. This was reiterated in 1934 and 1957. The intent was that the bonds would be paid off, the bridge would revert to the ownership of the two respective countries and the tolls would be reduced, if not eliminated. The tolls have not been reduced and I suspect they have been increased on more than one occasion. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary could provide information on this.
I believe there is other information for which we might ask and to which we should be entitled concerning the total annual revenue from tolls. Perhaps he would take the last few years, for example, and tell us whether the revenues have been sufficient to retire the debt and pay the interest and operational charges of the bridge. Also, we might be told whether there is any surplus because there is provision for any surplus to be divided equally between Canada and the United States.
Merchant Seamen Compensation Act
Then, perhaps we could be informed whether the original bond issue has been paid off. I suspect it has been paid off. It would be of interest to ascertain that, as well as the total amount of interest paid out. Then, we might be given information concerning the bond issues in 1934 and 1957. We would like to know the amount of the present bonded debt, the rate of interest in respect of each issue, when the bonds are due and whether the revenue from tolls is meeting the obligations in respect of debt retirement, maintenance, repairs and so on of the bridge itself.
Finally, I should like to return to my initial point and request that the Parliamentary Secretary provide the reasoning behind the perpetuation of this private company. He might tell us why the objective sought is to be achieved in this manner rather than through the bridge reverting to the ownership of the two countries. I will not call this a dummy company because I do not intend to be unkind, but it is an extra facility which I do not believe is necessary any longer. We do not intend to oppose the bill, but I believe it would be helpful if the Parliamentary Secretary could provide this information either now or at the committee stage.

that Bill C-188, to amend the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act and to amend an act to amend the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

December 1, 1970
Merchant Seamen Compensation Act
He said: Mr. Speaker, like many of the bills before us this afternoon this is a relatively minor bill in many respects but major in many others in that it has as its purpose amendment of the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act in three areas especially, if I recall correctly. First of all, the intent is to increase the scale of compensation presently provided under the act to seamen who are not covered by compensation in certain provinces in Canada, namely the Atlantic provinces. The reason they are not covered by provincial compensation is a rather historic one.
Generally speaking the purpose of the bill, as it presently stands, is to provide compensation for seamen from the Atlantic provinces who are not covered by provincial compensation acts. Since this act has been in existence for many years, a certain number of people received compensation as a result of accidents which occurred on the job. The one change that we would make of course, the obvious one, is to increase these rates of compensation to bring them in line with the compensation provided in the Atlantic provinces in those areas that are covered by Provincial compensation. Therefore, the scale of the new bill would be uniform with the highest scale in any of the Atlantic provinces at the present moment.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The second change that we are recommending in the bill is to provide for these periodic increases through the Governor in Council. The regulatory factor here is that the increases would always be in conformity with the increases that occur in the various provinces.
The third, and perhaps the more important, feature in the eyes of many people has been suggested to me by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave). On many occasions in the House of Commons, and particularly through correspondence, the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants has emphasized the need for broadening the definition of the word "accident" to include certain illnesses, if I may use that expression, that occur on the job, such as dermatitis and illnesses of this nature. Again, this is pretty well in conformity with the more enlightened legislation that exists in the provinces.
To repeat, the three areas that are covered by the bill are: first, to increase the benefits of compensation to the people covered by this act to bring them into conformity with the levels of compensation in the various provinces; second, to provide that we can keep pace with the necessary changes to this act through the Governor in Council rather than by bringing them back to the House each time; and third, to broaden the definition of "accident" in conformity with the wishes of the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants and in order to bring it into conformity with the legislation in other provinces.
I might remind the House that the cost for those already on compensation would come out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. It is rather nominal in amount, and of course the cost of compensation for future accidents and so forth will come from the employers of people covered by the act. I hope, therefore, in view of

the fact that the main purpose of this bill is to raise the benefits to people presently under the act and to those who may have the misfortune to come under the act in the future, this bill might receive a speedy passage. Possibly we could waive the necessity of going to the standing committee and have it accepted in committee of the whole this afternoon.

maintopic: MERCHANT SEAMEN COMPENSATION ACT

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the minister for his statement. So far as my party is concerned, we would be willing to adopt the course suggested by the minister.
The minister has put forward very fairly the three principal changes in the bill. I think it should be emphasized that until we, as a Parliament, act and pass the bill, the benefits that flow therefrom will not reach the people who are concerned. Therefore, there is an immediacy about it that I am sure appeals to hon. members who want quick remedies. I know that my associates will agree with me when I say that should it be desirable to go into committee of the whole immediately and have the bill cleared in the House of Commons today, there would be no objection from this side.
May I also say I am very pleased that the minister and the Merchant Seamen Compensation Board have listened to a representation that I made. The minister has been more than generous in his reference to me in that regard, but the representation came from a woman in Halifax, a Mrs. Joyce Tines whose husband some years ago was serving on a boat going into the Caribbean. He suffered an illness and died. The man died, not because he was hit by a falling boom or the like but because of some infection that had entered his body. Under the old act he was simply not eligible for compensation, although the fact that he had an illness had been just as accidental as if he had been hit by something. However, there was that legal difference and the widow did not collect compensation. I suppose she cannot collect it even now, although in future other people who suffer an illness when they serve as Canadian merchant seamen abroad will be compensated. We have not solved Mrs. Tines' problem directly but 1 think a large part of the act should be called the "Tines act" because she fought for a cause on behalf of others.
In conclusion, may I again thank the minister for his generosity. I support this bill and I hope we can deal expeditiously with it.

maintopic: MERCHANT SEAMEN COMPENSATION ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROTECTION, COMPENSATION, PAYMENTS TO WIDOWS AND DEPENDENT CHILDREN '
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I can say that I welcome this bill because of one feature of it in particular, that is the provision which will enable compensation rates to be suitably adjusted from time to time without direct reference to Parliament. If I remember correctly, this is about the third time I have been involved in a discussion of a bill similar to this one in respect of this particular act. The proposal for bringing the rates in line with those that are now generally prevailing under the various other compensation acts in the country is one that we can support.
I must say that a good point has been raised with particular reference to the broadening of the coverage. Apparently, a particular individual's problem must be
December 1, 1970

brought into the open before this can be accomplished. I am glad the minister has acted to bring forward this proposal which results from the circumstances that were described by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave). Certainly, the proposed broadening does not go beyond the normal terms that one expects in a compensation act. So far as my knowledge of British Columbia's law is concerned, any accident occurring in the course of or connected with the employment of an individual is deemed to be compensable. I think that if hon. members from the Atlantic coast, who are more knowledgeable of the details of the administration of this act, are satisfied with the suggestion that we deal with the bill expeditiously in committee of the whole, then from the general knowledge that I have of the act and the way it has functioned in the past I can see no objection to that procedure.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we now have before us Bill C-188, "An Act to amend the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act and to amend an Act to amend the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act".
The explanatory notes read in part as follows:
The purpose of this amendment is to broaden the circumstances in which protection is afforded under the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act to merchant seamen and their dependants to include circumstances where disablement arises out of and in the course of employment.
And with respect to clause 2 of the bill, it is stated:
The purpose of these amendments is to increase the amounts of compensation ... in respect of allowances for widows and dependent children of merchant seamen.
Mr. Speaker, we are aware that the people concerned by this bill have to face the cost of living which has reached an alarmingly high level and since they are in no way responsible for this increase, it is only fair and reasonable, in my opinion, that the government should proceed as it is doing now, through the minister, by introducing this bill in the House to enable these stricken people to avail themselves to a certain extent of this security to which they are entitled.
In view of all the opportunities which exist at all levels in this country, we know that Canadian production is high enough to allow each and every citizen to get his fair share without ever having to dread the future.
Because this measure will mainly benefit those seamen's widows and dependents, whether they have experienced the death of a kin or been sick or suffered an accident, we of the Ralliement creditiste shall consider it our duty to support this bill.

Mr. Speaker, hon. members may recall the government statement reporting to the House on the impact of concessional financing on Canadian interests and the measures the government proposed to use in mitigating its effects in so far as it causes injury to Canadian industry. One of these measures was amendment of the Anti-dumping Act, broadening the terms of reference of the Anti-dumping Tribunal to permit it to determine injury or threat of injury to Canadian producers from imports for causes other than dumping.
The term "concessional financing" describes the practice adopted by some foreign governments of guarantee-

December 1, 1970
Anti-Dumping Act
ing loans to Canadian borrowers at interest rates lower than commercial rates prevailing in the lender's home market in exchange for the borrower's commitment to purchase goods from producers in the country of the lending government.
Governments of most industrialized countries have provided facilities for financing exports for many years. Historically, government interest rates for such financing have been equal to, if not greater than, commercial rates Under these conditions government export financing did not have a significant influence on trade between developed countries where businessmen have access to efficient money markets. However, over the past few years interest rates on government export financing have increased less rapidly than commercial rates. Therefore, such financing has become more attractive to prospective borrowers, and they are willing to commit themselves to limit their purchasing to firms in the lending country m exchange for concessional credit terms. The effect of such purchase commitments made by Canadian borrowers is to limit Canadian producers' opportunities to supply the needs of the Canadian market. Therefore, the government has decided to take measures to mitigate injury caused to Canadian producers by concessional financing.
I should like to make it perfectly clear that the interest rate differential which is of concern is that between the rate offered through the facilities of a foreign government's export financing program and that which prevails in the commercial money market of the lending country. We realize that there will often be differences in rates between commercial markets in different countries. This latter difference is analogous to differences which occur internationally between costs of other resources, and as such is a normal feature of international trade.
One of the measures is embodied in clause 3 of Bill S-6 to amend the Anti-dumping Act. This clause provides that the terms of reference of the Anti-dumping Tribunal be changed to permit the Governor in Council to direct the tribunal to inquire into circumstances relating to the importation of any category of goods, and to determine whether or not such imports are causing or may cause injury to Canadian producers. The tribunal's present terms of reference provide that it may inquire into injury from imports only in so far as injury is caused by "dumping", that is, when the "export price" of goods is lower than the "normal value" of like goods in the country of export.
However, there are other categories of imports which may cause injury, such as those whose prices are affected by government subsidies, or those imported in large volume at very low prices in a short period of time which disrupt orderly growth of a market and have an adverse effect on both Canadian producers and on exporters to Canada who have already established a position in the Canadian market.
The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade recognizes the right of members to take action against such imports, and measures to permit such action are embodied in Canadian legislation. Specifically, the Canadian Customs Tariff provides that special duties may be
imposed on imports which are subsidized by the government of the exporting country (section 6), or which are imported under conditions which cause serious injury to Canadian producers (section 7). While the Canadian legislation is consistent with GATT, we are obliged to defend action taken under these provisions by providing proof that injury has been caused or is threatened by certain imports. At present, the proof of injury is determined by the Governor in Council on the advice of officials. The new terms of reference proposed for the tribunal will permit the tribunal to determine questions of injury on request of the Governor in Council.
There are three principal advantages to the course proposed. First, the tribunal has developed considerable expertise in ruling on questions of injury through its inquiries relating to dumping under the Anti-dumping Act. This expertise can be readily applied to a number of categories of imports which may cause injury and will ensure consistent application of injury criteria as between types of imports.
Second, the tribunal already has the authority to obtain all the data necessary to analyse particular import situations, and a mechanism for holding hearings and accepting formal representations. Finally, it is independent of conflicting pressures of departmental administration and is able to devote all its resources to assessment of injury.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
For these reasons, assignment of general responsibility for determination of injury to the Anti-Dumping Tribunal will increase the administrative effectiveness of these elements of our national trade policy and our ability to meet our obligations to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
During consideration of this bill by the Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce, members of the committee expressed concern that clause 3 as proposed did not clearly define the new terms of reference of the tribunal. The committee therefore recommended that the clause be redrafted to refer specifically to the tribunal's interest in "imports which might cause injury". The government has agreed to the suggested amendment in principle and I expect to propose an appropriate amendment for discussion in committee.
The bill also provides a number of technical amendments which have been included to clarify the wording of the present legislation in the light of experience gained in administering it. Most of the changes are selfexplanatory. However, I would like to make specific reference to one or two of them.
In the present act, subsection 3 of section 29, provides that the tribunal must not make public any information which would adversely affect the competitive position of parties to the injury. This provision ensures that parties to an anti-dumping investigation will be willing to provide the type of information required to permit a thorough inquiry by the tribunal. that Bill C-14 respecting tobacco as a health hazard, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said- Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity of presenting Bill C-14, respecting tobacco as a health hazard. This bill was on the order paper on a previous occasion but was not reached. This is the first time that a bill I have sponsored has been discussed on the floor of the House of Commons. I recall that two years ago some constituents of mine suggested it was a waste of time for private members to present bills. I can assure them now that this is not the case, because a bill of mine has come before the House and we now have the opportunity of discussing it.
The purpose of Bill C-14, respecting tobacco as a health hazard, is to make certain that tobacco and cigarette users are aware at all times that the use of these substances constitutes a health hazard. It is also proposed that a written and graphic warning be placed on all packages of tobacco and cigarettes. Clause 2 of the bill reads:
All packages of tobacco and cigarettes shall bear the words "Health Hazard-use at own risk" with a skull and cross-bones symbol thereunder, in a prominent place on the front of the package.
The report of the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare, which dealt with the subject of tobacco and cigarette smoking, reads in part as follows:
It is no longer in the public interest to prolong the debate about whether cigarette smoking is a health hazard.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel).]
There can be no question that if cigarettes were a food or a drug or newly marketed, their sale would have to be prohibited or strongly regulated on the basis of evidence now available.
The report continues:
It is perfectly obvious, however, that cigarettes cannot be banned today. Cigarette smoking is too widespread and is the basis of an economically important industry from grower through to retailer. Widespread illegal manufacture and distribution could be expected and economic hardship for growers, workers and others could follow a precipitous dismantling of the industry.
Consequently, there are two interests that must be balanced. The first is public health; the second is the protection of various segments of the tobacco industry. Let us first consider the question of the tobacco industry. The tobacco industry in Canada supplies full time employment to approximately 24,000 people. In addition, it supplies seasonal employment to 40,000 others. Every year in Canada the tobacco industry spends approximately $60 million on salaries for workers in the industry, pays $15 million for media advertising, spends $10 million on transportation costs and spends another $40 million on packaging materials and other supplies. In 1969, the total capital investment in Canadian tobacco farms was approximately $436 million. In 1968, of the total federal revenues, 6 per cent, or $555 million, was provided by the federal tobacco tax collections.
The other matter I now wish to consider is that of public health. On the public health side, cigarette smoking is one of the leading causes of preventable disease in Canada. According to the Report on Tobacco and Cigarette Smoking, 1969-70 of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, "cigarette smoking seems to be the dominant factor in the production of lung cancer and chronic bronchitis and emphysema", and is "an important risk factor in the development of coronary heart disease." The 1969 United States government supplement on health consequences linked smoking to coronary disorders, chronic bronchitis, pulmonary emphysema, throat and respiratory cancer and non-cancerous diseases of the mouth.
The risk of a fatal heart attack among the middle aged is two to three times greater for smokers than non smokers. Average male smokers have a ten times greater risk of lung cancer than non-smokers. Average male smokers have a six times greater death rate from chronic bronchitis and emphysema than non-smokers. I submit that these figures are irrefutable and ought to be taken into account in the consideration of this bill.
In 1968, the Department of National Health and Welfare estimated that a minimum of 10,000 Canadians die unnecessarily each year because of cigarette induced diseases-mainly heart attacks, lung cancer, chronic bronchitis and emphysema.
In October, 1970, the chief medical adviser for the British government reported that 100,000 Britons per year were being killed by cigarettes. In August, 1970, a study by a Berkley demographer indicated that smoking may be the strongest factor in the cessation of the trend toward longer life expectancy for western man. In January, 1970, a Japanese study revealed that Canadians are
December 1, 1970

the second heaviest smokers in the world, second only to Americans.
The 1964 report of the Advisory Committee to the Surgeon General of the United States reported that death rates for smokers of cigarettes only are about 70 per cent higher than those for non-smokers and increase with the amount smoked. For those who smoke less than 10 cigarettes per day, the death rate, as compared with that of non-smokers, is 40 per cent higher. For those who smoke between 10 and 19 cigarettes per day the death rate is 70 per cent higher. For those who smoke between 29 and 39 cigarettes per day, it is 90 per cent higher, and for those who smoke 40 or more cigarettes per day, the death rate is 120 per cent higher than it is for non-smokers. Once again, Mr. Speaker, I submit that these are irrefutable statistics and ought to be considered carefully.
A study by the Canadian Department of National Health and Welfare entitled "Trends in Death Rates from Diseases of Interest in Relation to Smoking in Canada: 1950 to 1966", concluded that although in this period over-all mortality in Canada was reduced, "arteriosclerotic heart disease (including coronary) lung cancer, chronic bronchitis and emphysema all showed a marked increase in crude mortality during this period for both the male and female population." The study went on to say that, "recent excess mortality for these diseases was related to smoking".
On January 1, 1966, by virtue of the United States Federal Cigarette Labelling and Advertising Act, all cigarettes manufactured, imported or packaged for sale or distribution within the United States were required to carry the following warning: "Caution: Cigarette Smoking May be Hazardous to Your Health". Since that time this warning has proven to be too weak and ineffective.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that, given the obvious danger to health presented by cigarette smoking, given the educational program of the Department of National Health and Welfare to combat smoking and given the recommendation of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs that cautions be placed on packages of cigarettes as part of this educational program, it is recommended that the written warning, "Health Hazard-use at own risk" be placed on all cigarette packages manufactured or sold in Canada and that this warning be accompanied by a graphic warning m tile form of a skull and crossbones. I submit that this symbol is vitally necessary to reinforce the written warning which has not proven effective in the United States. I hope that the minister will agree to the suggestions made in this bill, and that there will be unanimous support throughout the House for the bill to be passed at the earliest possible ime.

Beyond economic considerations, there is man himself. We can never forget that in the end it is a question of health, happiness and life for countless number of productive Canadians. The surest way of avoiding the smoking habit is obviously never to start and to endorse the slogan "unlit cigarette, harmless cigarette".
I do not expect to see most inveterate smokers renounce their habit from one day to the next, although if they did I would be very happy.
Nevertheless it is among young people who have not yet started to smoke that lie our best chances of success. Statistics concerning youth are very interesting: Canada 50 per cent of Canadian men aged 15 and over smoke cigarettes; among women the rate is about 33 per cent.
Now let us look at some figures regarding young people. In the age group from 15 to 19 years, 35 per cent of the boys and 21 per cent of the girls are regular smokers. In fact, this figure is rather lower than it should be because even if educators and parents are systematically opposed to this addiction, it is often indulged in secretly. Most smokers contract the habit in their teens and if we succeed in lowering this percentage our efforts will not have been in vain.
_ For several years the department has been compaign-ing against tobacco. It has been especially preoccupied with youth. This program was to a large degree educational since we tried to convince smokers to stop smoking and non smokers to abstain from starting to do it by showing them the risks tobacco is to health. We think that we have succeeded in a way.
The smoking habit is so deeply rooted that the prohibition of cigarettes would not give any result and would also be an attack against individual freedom. Furthermore, we cannot encourage our young people to develop the syndrome of forbidden fruit. Even if cigarette smoking is prohibited in secondary schools, statistics show, as we know, that this habit is spread among students attending such institutions.
If because of us the use of cigarettes became a forbidden pleasure, we would only incite a greater number of people to try this experience. Mr. Speaker, you may have been yourself the victim of secret smoking sessions.
As for me, I think that the Canadian people must remain free to smoke or not to smoke. We only want to encourage the public not to smoke and if they must do so, we urge them to run as little risk as possible. This is the underlying reason for our present education programme.
The effort made in order to solve the problem of cutting down the consumption of cigarettes must aim at protecting the public at large. And I think that such is the philosophy of the Department of National Health and Welfare in this field.
Tobacco Health Hazard Act
It is up to the government to protect Canadians and, particularly, to put them before the following fact: it is obvious that if a danger exists in a certain segment of society, it is the government's duty to protect the people.
Although it is obvious that the sale of cigarettes cannot be prohibited at the present time, it is equally obvious that the production, distribution and sale of cigarettes cannot be considered in the same perspective as production, distribution and sale of other products. It seems reasonable at this stage to use any practical measure to help phase out sales promotion. At the same time, plans must be made to help producers and other persons who will be adversely affected by the ban on the sale of cigarettes.
Increased education of the public, as a deterrent to smokers, would be desirable, as well as efforts to make cigarette smoking less dangerous for inveterate smokers.
It has been claimed that if cigarette smoking is harmful sale of the product should be completely prohibited and that otherwise it would be neither constitutional nor legal to interfere with sales promotion. However, plain common sense dictates that prohibiting the sale of cigarettes would not serve public interest. It must be admitted that cigarette smoking is in a class by itself among Canada's social and health problems. Society is therefore justified in seeking out unusual solutions and rejecting any argument based on technical considerations. It is clearly against the interest of society to promote actively the use of a harmful product, even though prohibition of its production and sale may be unacceptable.
Public opinion is becoming more vocal every day, pressing for practical action to reduce the health hazard resulting from the use of cigarettes by Canadians. This concern has been shown unequivocally with respect to cigarette advertising.
It has been argued ever so often that cigarette smoking is a matter of free choice on the part of reasonable adults. This is true inasmuch as a person is, in the final analysis, responsible for what he wants to do with his own body. It is also true, nevertheless, that if cigarette smoking has become such a generalized practice, it is due to the fact that it is habit-forming to a certain extent. In fact, we all know that a major proportion of cigarette sales is accounted for by the fact that cigarettes are sold to people who are unable to stop smoking. Apparently, there are various degrees of dependence which may be explained by reference to pharmacological, social and psychological factors. In any event, the cigarette habit appears in the case of many heavy smokers as eliminating any freedom of choice.
It should be mentioned that despite limited funds, Canadian programs on the effects of tobacco on health are expanding and that a great number of Canadians, convinced that cigarette smoking is a health hazard, strongly wish that measures be taken in that respect.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, we must be logical and support the measures which society will take to solve the

We could hardly expect, for instance, our youth to be convinced that governments think that the use of tobacco is really hazardous when at the same time they allow unrestricted advertising of cigarettes.
Furthermore, a great many smokers would like to break the habit or have resolved to quit. This is why we must do everything we can to encourage them and to make smoking which is part of modern society less attractive.

I do not quarrel with the suggestion that this is a large amount of money, and certainly anything that makes money for the country might be justified in the eyes of some. I also would not argue with the fact that there would be a loss from a damaged tobacco industry should a bill of this nature be passed. I would not argue with the fact that in Ontario 3,774 farmers might experience financial difficulty as the result of the passage of legislation such as this by the House of Commons.
Most people in the country realize that many Canadians depend on the production of tobacco for their livelihood. There is in this brief a picture of an area of the country that used to look like a desert, with little sand dunes all over the place, a barren territory with a horse and buggy rolling across and the wind blowing sand all over. In the picture below it there is a beautiful farm with tobacco fields and little huts standing in a row where the tobacco is cured. This is certainly nice, but I am not convinced by these arguments.
The tobacco industry is in effect saying that for the purpose of making a profit we are willing to sacrifice health and years of human life. When we consider this matter we must look at these statistics very seriously. There are many statistics available and many research studies that have been conducted in this area. I do not think there is any doubt that the usage of cigarettes is harmful to health. As a matter of fact, it has been worked out in detail to the point where we are told that every cigarette a smoker uses shortens his life by seven minutes. The average person using a package of cigarettes a day from age 25 stands to lose an average of 8 to 10 years of life expectancy.
The hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand may know many people who are old and who have smoked all their lives. All I can say is that if they had lived to age 90 and smoked, they might have lived to age 120 had they not smoked. We also hear the argument that other things such as liquor are much worse than tobacco. Supporting this bill does not mean we are supporting the use of alcohol or saying that its use is less harmful than tobacco. Perhaps everyone would admit that the use of alcohol is very harmful and should be discouraged as much as possible, perhaps to an even greater extent than tobacco. We could also mention other substances such as bread, animal fats, cheese or any number of things; used in large quantities, they can have harmful side effects. It is well known that the use of animal fat in large quantities contributes very greatly to arteriosclerosis, coronary heart disease and those other things which are great killers in our nation today. At the same time, the fact that we are using these substances does not justify perpetuating the use of tobacco.
I should like to describe a patient I have in my care, Mr. Speaker. He is a man about 65 years of age who was a farmer. He had been using cigarettes to the extent of about a package a day for most of his adult life. About five years ago he began to complain about shortness of breath. When he ran after the cow he found she could outrun him because he was too short of breath.
