I believe research in this area is lacking. Much more effort is required in order to bring about some kind of a solution.
As has been suggested, people who have the smoking habit should be discouraged in respect of the use to tobacco through education programs among the youth and also among adults. It might be desirable to encourage people to develop other habits. Some people might suggest smoking hashish. It would seem that the federal goverment is promoting the replacement of tobacco by the use of marijuana. I do not believe I would approve of this because there is no research which indicates that marijuana will not produce the same harmful effects to
Tobacco Health Hazard Act
the lungs of people. It might well produce emphysema, bronchitis and all the other illnesses and diseases about which hon. members have spoken.
I am receiving many suggestions but I do not think I should repeat some of them. One member said there are in the order of 60,000 deaths in Canada per year because of tobacco usage. This would seem to indicate a tremendously serious problem. We cannot afford to lose 60,000 people because of failure to act in an area which is entirely preventable.
I suggest that an alternative use might be found for the product of the tobacco producers and manufacturers and that alternatives might be found for people who smoke tobacco, such as scratching their heads or twiddling their thumbs. I do not know, however, how enjoyable or satisfying this would be. I believe that about a year ago the CBC ceased tobacco advertising on television. At that time there seemed to be an outcry to the effect that a tremendous amount of revenue would be lost. I do not believe this revenue has been lost, because the CBC has found alternative advertising. If this could be done in respect of the CBC, then surely it could be done just as well in respect of the farmers, manufacturers and distributors of tobacco.
I do not wish to talk out this bill, because I support it. I would point out one interesting fact about my hon. friend who spoke against this bill. He does not use cigarettes; he only smokes cigars. Research would seem to indicate that cigars do not produce the same amount of cancer, bronchitis, emphysema, and so on, that cigarettes do. Someone might ask whether these other substances are less harmful. As I believe was shown by the witnesses who appeared before our committee last year, it is not merely a question of whether or not one uses cigarettes, because there are many other factors which come into play. One is the question of whether or not a person inhales. It would appear that people who start smoking cigars from the beginning do not necessarily develop the habit of inhaling as much as do those who smoke cigarettes. From the research available now, there would seem to be fewer cases of pulmonary disease and lung cancer among cigar and pipe smokers.
However, in respect of persons who formerly had been cigarette smokers and switched to cigars or a pipe, it does not make much difference because virtually all cigarette smokers inhale every puff and generally speaking when they switch to cigars or a pipe they continue to inhale. Therefore, switching in itself does not make too much difference. So far as chewing tobacco and taking snuff are concerned, I do not believe there has been sufficient study in respect of these products to reach any very conclusive opinion. I believe the incidence of pulmonary disease would be reduced with the usage of these two products because they are not inhaled and, therefore, the nicotine and hot gas is not taken down the throat. There has been some suggestion that the use of these products could lead to cancer of the mouth and throat, and so on, so I do not believe they really are substitutes.
In conclusion, I reiterate that I am merely putting the facts before the House as I see them, and I am not

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon we have had a very severe condemnation of ciga-reites and whisky, which leaves but one other and that is wild, wild women. I have no intention of condemning the vice or whatever it is called, of wild, wild women. In respect of the bill presented by the hon. member for Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson), who is a very good friend of mine, I want to say the intent is good. I shall play the devil's advocate this afternoon and ask whether the bill and the remedies proposed would do any good.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
First, the hon. member said there is irrefutable evidence that cigarettes produce lung cancer, emphysema, and so on. I, too, was a member of the committee and I will bring to the attention of hon. members the evidence presented by Dr. Hans Selye. He said that the greatest contributing factor to all these diseases, and especially to' cancer, is stress. I asked him: "Dr. Selye, how would you recognize a man who is constantly living under undue stress? Does he chew nails?" Dr. Selye agreed he would chew nails. I asked: "Would he have a nervous tic?" Dr. Selye agreed he would. Then I asked: "But what is the most common symptom of stress?" I was told that cigarette smoking was the most common symptom; it is evidence of a man under undue stress. The question then arises: Is it the cigarette that kills the man, or is it stress? Smoking cigarettes is evidence that the man is under stress.

subtopic: PROVISION RESPECTING WARNING LABEL
speechtext: It is cigarette smoking that causes stress.

maintopic: TOBACCO HEALTH HAZARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION RESPECTING WARNING LABEL
speechtext:
Babies have colic. Babies drink milk. Therefore, milk produces colic. This is the same type of argument. I am not sure that it is indeed cigarette smoking or the use of the pipe or tobacco that does this harm. I think it is evidence of the fact that there is stress. I accept Dr. Selye's evidence, a man who is well known throughout the world for his studies in this field.
Before I rose to speak, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Isabelle) gave me several sheets of paper and said, "Here is your speech". He knows better than that. The introduction reads, "Mr. Speaker", I will go that far. The rest indicates that certain studies are being followed by the department. I am glad to see they are not so much on what sort of diseases might be caused by cigarette smoking but are, rather, on how to give up smoking.
This is the issue I wish to raise this afternoon. The bill points out how we should go about this. It recommends that there be a warning that cigarette smoking is a health hazard, in the form of a skull and crossbones. If you were an entrepreneur, what brand of cigarettes would you come up with? I know what I would do, I would come up with a skull and crossbones brand. One could not have anything better; every package would have your advertisement on it.

Then there is this business of whether or not cigarettes are a health hazard. I would remind the hon. member for Lakeshore that some time ago the Ontario government passed a bill in connection with the used car business. The bill stated that every car sold from a used car lot had to have a certificate stating whether or not it was roadworthy. In other words, if you sell a car you have to issue a certificate stating whether or not the car is roadworthy. Since that time every certificate for every car sold has contained the statement, in half-inch letters, that the car is or is not roadworthy. Nevertheless, everyone is buying these cars; it has not seemed to affect sales.
It is a curious quirk of human nature that although everyone knows that cigarettes are bad for them and that they might kill people, people do not apply this knowledge to themselves. It only seems to apply to others. This is the saving grace of mankind. One believes it is only dangerous to the health of others. Having said what I have said, I cannot believe that cigarettes are good. No one can convince me that the inhalation of smoke is harmless, because it must have some ill effects.
The question, then, is: How are we going to stop the use of cigarettes, or how are we going to stop their promotion? In so far as the report of the committee went, it was good, presuming that people behave like angels. But the truth is that people are not angels; we are human beings subject to all sorts of pressures and all sorts of promotional gimmicks. If you stop advertising on radio and television, there will be a switch to newspapers and magazines. If you stop that, there will be promotion of car racing, skiing, and so on. If you stop that, there will be contests with lots of nice prizes. If you stop that, there will be something else.
The only way is to hit the businessman, the promoter or manufacturer of cigarettes where it hurts. I have recommended this to the government several times. It is not fair that we should all pay half the advertising costs. The manufacturer of cigarettes writes off all his advertising and promotional expenses against his profits. In other words, 50 per cent is paid by the government. It is very simple to stop that. All the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has to do is say that from this day onward advertising and promotion of cigarettes will not be a deductible expense. That would do away with all this nonsense. If people want to advertise cigarettes, let them do so out of their own pocket.
I am a great believer in the power of the purse in so far as consumers are concerned. There is no easier way than to raise taxes on cigarettes, nor is anything justifiable. One dollar for a package of cigarettes would not be unjustifiable. If you want to smoke cigarettes, pay $1 a package. If that is not enough, pay $1.50. This is a workable process. Nothing would compel a man to break away from the habit more than the pocket-book telling him of the many things he could buy with the money even if it were whisky.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is little more than a year since we debated a bill on anti-dumping matters following very extensive examination resulting from a white paper on the subject. Some people might be inclined to be critical of the fact that having gone through the white paper process and having voted on and dealt with a bill on this subject, we see after such a short interval a new bill introduced proposing amendments to the previous legislation. However, I am inclined to think it is rather a good thing that the government is moving so quickly.
The subject is a complicated one. It is obvious that certain things have occurred since the previous legislation was passed that give rise to some of the proposed amendments. Based on my examination of the bill, I believe there are two main items in it. There are some cleaning-up items and two major changes, both of which I think are satisfactory.
We will have a greater opportunity in the Standing Committee to look at the proposed changes, but for the moment I believe the proposal to provide for an inquiry initiated by the Governor in Council is an important one. Very often some of the people who may wish to initiate an inquiry are involved in rather delicate negotiations with various governments with regard to concessional financing, and thus might find it difficult to initiate an inquiry. Proposed new section 16A would seem to give the Governor in Council power to call such an inquiry on examination of a certain situation that might be brought to its attention, or that might arise in connection with
Farm Improvement Loans Acts another investigation conducted by it. It is worth while to have this kind of power enshrined in legislation and at the moment I am inclined to support it.
The second important matter concerns confidential evidence. In committee we took the position that we could not find much reason why so much of the evidence had to be confidential. We are still inclined to wonder about the degree of secrecy that surrounds many inquiries and many business dealings in this country. However, our view did not prevail and the restriction with respect to confidentiality was written into the legislation. Now it appears that there are some loopholes with respect to confidential evidence, depending on how evidence is given to the tribunal. The provisions of clauses 6 and 7 seem to be an attempt to make sure that at least the principle of confidentiality is preserved, regardless of how evidence is given to or obtained by the tribunal. Mr. Speaker, we are prepared to see the bill go to committee for further examination.

maintopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENT PROVIDING ADDITIONAL THREE-YEAR LOAN PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-191 proposes amendments to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act and the Small Businesses Loans Act. These acts, which are well known to hon. members, enable the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) to guarantee term loans made by the chartered banks and other designated financial institutions to farmers, fishermen and small businessmen to finance a wide variety of capital improvement projects in connection with their business enterprises. Under the existing provisions of each act, these programs will expire on June 30 of next year and the main purpose of Bill C-191 is to provide for the continuation of these programs for a further three years to June 30, 1974.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Before discussing the provisions of this bill, I would like to comment on each program. The Farm Improvement Loans Act was implemented in 1944, initially for a three-year period. It has been amended on numerous occasions to add new lending periods and to enlarge the benefits available to farmers qualifying under the act. Presently, farmers may borrow up to $15,000 to help finance the acquisition of farm implements, buildings,

December 1, 1970
Farm Improvement Loans Acts
equipment or livestock and to repair or improve assets which are used in their farming enterprises. In addition, farmers may borrow up to $15,000 for the purchase of additional land. This purpose, which was included in the act in 1968, allows farmers to purchase small parcels of land to round out an existing farm unit. Both of these limits are subject to an over-all maximum of $25,000 which .a farmer may have outstanding at any one time for all loan purposes.
The maximum period over which repayment may be spread varies with the purpose for which the loan was obtained and ranges from three years in the case of trucks to 15 years in the case of land purchase loans. That the Farm Improvement Loans Act has played a crucial role in the financing of Canadian agriculture is evidenced by the fact that over $2 billion has been loaned during the quarter century of operations under the act. Lending reached a peak in 1966 and during 1969, the last full year of operations, approximately $142 million were loaned under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Claims paid under this program have been remarkably low and amount to just over one-tenth of one per cent of the face value of loans made.
The Fisheries Improvement Loans Act came into effect in 1955, also for an initial three-year period, and has subsequently been expanded and amended from time to time. Under the current provisions of the act, fishermen may borrow up to $25,000 to help finance the purchase, construction or repair of fishing vessels and equipment. The development of shore installations and equipment which are a necessary part of a fishing enterprise is also an eligible loan purpose. Borrowers may take up to ten years to repay most loans, although in the case of loans for certain purposes the maximum repayment period is shorter, more closely approximating the useful life of the asset being acquired. Lending under this program occurred at relatively low levels for several years. More recently, however, there has been a notable increase. In the year ending March 31, 1970, fisheries improvement loans reached a peak and amounted to $2.6 million. Claims have been very low under this program, totalling only $13,400 since inception.
The Small Businesses Loans Act came into effect in early 1961 for a three-year period. This legislation provides for loans of up to $25,000 to assist small businessmen in financing improvements in their business enterprises. In order to qualify, an enterprise must have gross revenues of less than $500,000 and must be engaged in one of the following forms of business activity- manufacturing, retail or wholesale trade, provision of services, construction, transportation or communications. Loans may be used to assist in acquiring fixed or movable equipment or for the purchase, construction or renovation of business premises. Since inception, more than $200 million has been made available to small businesses under the provisions of this legislation. Lending in recent years has been below the peak levels reached in 1964 and 1965 and amounted to $16 million in 1969. Losses under this legislation have also been small-less than one-half of one per cent of the total value of loans made.
A number of general provisions apply in connection with loans made under each of the programs. Borrowers are required to pledge security for loans, generally by way of a charge on the assets acquired with the loan and by giving a promissory note. In certain circumstances, additional security may be required by the lender. Potential borrowers must also be prepared to make a minimum investment of their own in the project for which they seek a loan. There is also a maximum rate of interest which lenders may charge on loans. Until the recent past, the maximum rate of interest which could be charged on loans was fixed either by statute or l'egulation at 5 per cent for farm improvement loans and fisheries improvement loans, and 5 per cent in the case of business improvement loans. These rates came to be increasingly unrealistic in view of the upward trend in the general level of interest rates, with the result that lenders found it difficult to make loans under these programs.
Changes have been approved whereby maximum interest rates are now determined semi-annually on April 1 and October 1 of each year. The rates are based on the average yields of selected government of Canada bonds over a six-month period to which is added a margin of 1 per cent. The maximum rate which can be charged during the period which commenced on October 1 of this year is 8 per cent for loans made under the Small Businesses Loans Act, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act for all loan purposes except the purchase of additional land. The maximum rate for land purchase loans, currently 8J per cent, is determined by a slightly different formula designed to reflect the longer time that may be taken to repay these loans.
As I indicated earlier, the essential purpose of Bill C-191 is to provide for a continuation of these lending programs for a three-year period beyond June 30, 1971. An amendment is proposed, therefore, to add to each act a new three-year lending period to extend to June 30, 1974.
The bill also establishes the aggregate principal amount of guaranteed loans which may be made by all lenders in the new lending periods. For the Farm Improvement Loans Act it is proposed that the maximum be set at the same level which is in effect during the current three-year lending period. The proposed ceiling is $900 million in respect of loans made by the chartered banks and $300 million for loans made by all other designated lenders. The guaranteed loan amounts in the current lending period for the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act-July 1, 1970, to June 30, 1971-are $10 million for the chartered banks and $10 million for other lenders. It is proposed to double the amount for the chartered banks to $20 million but leave unchanged the limit in respect of other lenders. The increase for the banks is proposed in response to the growth in their lending which has occurred in the past four years.
The current lending period under the Small Businesses Loans Act extends from January 1, 1970, to June 30, 1971, and the limitation on the aggregate principal amount of guaranteed loans which may be made is $100

December 1, 1970

million and $50 million for chartered banks and other lenders respectively. For the new period, these ceilings will be doubled to $200 million and $100 million, reflecting the fact that the new period will be three years whereas the current period is a year and one-half.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize that these measures have been instrumental in the provision of intermediate and longer term loan funds for farmers, fishermen and small businessmen. The government bel eves that the continuation of these programs for a further three-year period is desirable and should significantly contribute to increased economic expansion and efficiency on the part of the borrowers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in the official opposition propose to put up a number of speakers to deal with each of the subjects covered by this bill-the agricultural community, small business and the fishermen. For my part, Mr. Speaker, I would like to confine my remarks to agricultural loans. One could not help but follow with inlerest the history of loans to the agribusiness as outlined by the previous speaker. He traced the loans program from its origin through to the present day, ending with the proposed amendment to extend it for yet another three years.
Mr. Speaker, the original intent of this legislation was to make guaranteed loans available to the farming community at a low, fixed rate of interest in order that the industry could expand. The loans were to be used to encourage the renovation of farms being purchased by veterans and young men entering the agricultural industry and to amalgamate small units into larger, more viable ones. The money was used also in an attempt by the farming industry to improve and modernize production methods so that Canadian farmers could successfully vie with their competitors.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
The previous speaker said that the success of the program is indicated by the fact that during the past 20 or 25 years approximately $2 billion were borrowed by people in the business of farming. The government is now limiting the aggragate of all such loans to $1,200 million. But I think the greatest indication of what is happening is the fact that these loans are falling off. The previous speaker indicated that farming people during the last 12 months borrowed approximately $145 million.
This shows, I think, that a very serious change in attitude is taking place in the agribusiness with regard to the help proferred by the government. These loans are no longer the tools in the hands of farmers that they were some years ago, and for two reasons. The first and basic reason is that no longer do the basic qualifications as laid down originally tell a man whether or not he is eligible for a loan. Very often a man does not know whether or not he may procure a loan. Not long ago, when farmers approached the authorized lending institutions they found to their amazement that no matter whether they qualified for a loan or not, they could not obtain one. The
Farm Improvement Loans Acts
excuse given was that if the lending institutions were to lend, money to sectors other than the agribusiness, a higher rate of interest could be procured.
Many farmers who went to lending institutions expecting to borrow money at 5 per cent, the rate of interest prescribed by law for farm improvement and similar loans, were told that the money was not available but that if they wished to take out a bank loan at a higher rate of interest, it would be forthcoming. That was said even though they might have qualified for a lower-cost loan under government regulations. It was found that the money just was not available.
Not until the government in its wisdom took off the 5 per cent interest ceiling and allowed the rates charged on these loans to be comparable with other lending rates did the money once more flow into the farming industry Th,s action, however, destroyed one of the main reasons why farmers had utilized these low-cost loans to such a great extent. They had been able to obtain money at lower rates of interests than those prevailing in the maiket, and that advantage disappeared.
There is another reason why the number of loans made and the desire for loans is dwindling. This reason has important and tragic consequences for the farming community. The experience of farmers, especially in the last two years, has been that government departments are at odds one with another in the policy being put forward with respect to the agricultural industry. Farmers who with great confidence borrowed sums of money to extend their holdings, improve their equipment and develop more viable farms, found to their dismay and alarm that the government had entered into policies which made it impossible for them to repay these loans.
Men who borrowed money to build a more competitive dairy farm found that government policy was designed to curtail the production of dairy commodities in Canada Men who borrowed money to extend their production of primary produce found, suddenly, that the government ad either withdrawn its subsidy on certain commodities or had curtailed them to such a degree as to lower profit margins or eliminate them entirely. Therefore, it is not surprising that farmers do not wish to borrow.
I think one of the greatest indications of the manner in which the agricultural community has reacted to the benevolence of the government is this. The increase in the estimated value of the capital assets of agriculture in Canada over the past 15 years has been almost identical to total borrowings, under the provisions of these laws from government-authorized sources. In other words, Mr! Speaker, farmers have learned the hard way that borrowing this money does not solve their problems in the mam. With dwindling profit margins and with the prospect of government policies that seem directed exclusively at the concept of supply management and production controls, no farmer today can confidently predict what wiH be produced even three years hence, let alone whether he will be allowed to produce certain commodities. In these circumstances, unfortunate though they may
December 1, 1970

Farm Improvement Loans Acts be, farmers are not encouraged to take advantage of these loans.
I am not surprised that the government is extending the program for three years. We in this party support these amendments but we do not feel confident that they will solve the difficulties of farmers. These loans are a vehicle of last resort for farmers who believe that by obtaining this sort of addition to their working capital they will correct some of the economic deficits which will face them in the future. It is not with any confidence that we approach the amendments, but it is with a sense of foreboding because we know full well that they will not solve the difficulties of our agricultural community. Of course, that is a matter of opinion. The allocation of more debt money for the Canadian agricultural community, which apparently is destined to face a rocky future in the years immediately ahead, leads one to believe that agriculture today in Canada has much to fear.

maintopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENT PROVIDING ADDITIONAL THREE-YEAR LOAN PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has been noted, the bill before us amends the Small Businesses Loans Act, the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. It extends the term of their operations for another three years and also extends the limits of the guarantees set out in the legislation. Other members of the New Democratic Party will be dealing with this bill in terms of its specific application to the agricultural and fishing industries in particular. There are a number of general comments that I should like to make about this legislation, which I feel are very relevant at this time, as we consider the bill at second reading stage.
I think it may be fairly noted, Mr. Speaker, that the scope of this legislation is such that it is designed to provide services to a group of people within the Canadian economy who might be termed as the independent people in the economy. For the most part, those people are declining in numbers; there is a smaller and smaller number of them each year. I think some important decisions will have to be made by Canada in the near future with respect to the people who are engaged in farming, fishing and small businesses.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
We have to consider the future of these people, the services they require and the production they carry out at the present time in the sectors of the economy for which they are responsible. The bill before us may appear to be innocuous in many respects. It may appear mechanical and somewhat automatic in that it simply changes a few dates and makes a few other very minor changes. If we examine this bill we will see that this is not so I suggest that it implies a continuation of policies which are now in effect, or the absence of policies as they apply to farmers, fishermen and small businessmen.
In many respects these policies or lack of policies have not worked in terms of serving the well-being and welfare of these groups within the economy, because there has been a constant drain of people from these various
[Mr. Danforth.l
sectors, a drain which has not been a rational sort of movement or adjustment; it has occurred in a very irrational, haphazard way. This movement and adjustment is being made in the most painful possible way. This adjustment involves hardship and suffering for many thousands of Canadians in various parts of Canada. This particular economic sector involves continuing depressed conditions in many areas.
Many people who earn their living in occupations such as farming, fishing and small business are faced with depressed conditions. In many instances they earn below average incomes. The people engaged in these forms of livelihood often form the core of poverty problems in many areas of Canada. Each of these economic sectors is faced with problems. Small businesses are often faced with a capital shortage and difficulty in competing with large corporate enterprises. Very often there are institutional problems involving restrictions on the types of products that can be handled, services that can be provided and arrangements with distributors. There is a great deal of difficulty when small businessmen try to provide the type of service they want to provide the customers they serve.
Farmers are faced with a chronic situation involving low prices. A variety of market problems have plagued agriculture in Canada for many years. Many farmers are not only faced with competition in the market, but with competition from governments in other countries in terms of subsidies provided to agriculture in other parts of the world. There is a considerable lack of similar support to farmers in this country. Fishermen have a variety of problems involving prices and markets as well as the current problem of pollution.
All of the groups we are considering this evening are faced with problems involving technology and its influence on our society. Technology is forcing change and adjustment in the world. It is not a question of whether we are going to change, but of how this change is going to take place. What is going to happen? What sort of change will finally result? What will be the end result of the adjustments that are going to take place?
These changes can take place in two different ways. They can take place in an unplanned, destructive and insensitive manner which ignores human needs, community problems and other needs of the Canadian society. On the other hand, these changes can be effected through planning which considers human, social needs and the needs of communities throughout Canada. It involves a determination of objectives, a determination of what we want to do, how we want the various sectors of economy to develop and what role they are to fulfil in Canadian society.
What has the government done with respect to the programs within the scope of this bill? They have charged the borrower, whether he is a farmer, fisherman or small businessman, the current market rate of interest. The current market rate of interest has developed within the restricted market framework. In other words, we have influence on the marketplace because of the limited sources of capital available for borrowing purposes in
December 1, 1970

terms of the sources of this capital. When the farmers, fishermen and small businessmen try to sell their produce or services they are left at the mercy of a market system that no longer operates on a competitive basis.
These groups of people operate within a framework which does not enable them to compete effectively and equally with other sectors of the Canadian economy. This is the basis upon which many thousands of Canadians must attempt to earn their livelihood. Credit programs alone will not solve the problems faced by the various groups. Past experience has proven that credit programs, however valuable and important a role they play-and no one would underrate or underestimate the importance of capital as a tool in effecting adjustment and in equipping these various groups to make a more effective contribution to the economy-have not done the job.
To be effective, programs must be complemented by other programs. This requires a comprehensive program involving the adoption of planning-not a form of planning imposed from the top down but planning which involves people and communities in determining their future. They must be equipped with the necessary resources to reach their objectives and the role in life which they desire. We must take a close look at our communities. What type of communities do we want in the future? Many thousands of communities in Canada rely on farming, fishing and small businessmen in order to remain viable. The future of many of these communities is threatened at the present time. The people do not know what is going to happen to their community in the future. The outlook is uncertain because of the concern in many parts of Canada due to the absence of government programs.
We have to develop rational structures in the various economic sectors with which we are concerned tonight, structures which consider the needs of people and communities. I can give a number of examples regarding my own province of Saskatchewan, with which I am most familiar, which require consideration. We must examine this legislation and other complementary programs that need to be developed if this legislation is to perform a useful and effective function. Many people living in the urban areas of Saskatchewan earn their living through some form of small commercial enterprise such as a general store, grocery store, farm implement agency, garage or service station. Many of these businesses are threatened. The people do not know what will exist in the future. They do not know what will happen to their community. A variety of public and government services are being withdrawn from their communities-railway station agents, post offices and a consolidation program anticipated by some elevator companies. These businessmen feel insecure. They are naturally concerned about what is likely to happen to them.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
If this legislation is to serve a useful role it must be complemented by other programs which will further help small businessmen, farmers and fishermen whose interests this bill is intended to serve. In my own province of Saskatchewan many small businessmen feel most uncer-
Farm Improvement Loans Acts tain about their future. One reason for this is the lack of any effective form of community planning which takes into account the needs of those who make their living in the community and the kind of services they require. I realize that this calls for provincial legislation as well, but I contend that more effective controls should be applied to private industries and corporations to provide some services to the small communities I have in mind.
Let me give one example of what I mean. At present many small farm implement dealers throughout western Canada are being forced to the wall. For a variety of reasons they cannot continue to operate. The fact is they can carry only one line of machinery; in order to do business they are obliged to take out a franchise and this limits them to carrying one particular line of machinery. In today's world, this is not good enough. The system does not meet the needs of communities I have in mind. Hundreds of small communities in the rural areas are without the service of a farm machinery dealer because of the conditions laid down by the industry in line with its own business and competitive situation. Many of the farmers cannot obtain adequate service; they cannot buy the new farm machinery they require through a local dealer; they cannot obtain necessary parts and other services needed to carry on operations.
I could go on to deal at greater length with the situation of farmers and fishermen who I believe to be facing serious problems, but I do not intend to go into detail since some of my hon. friends will be dealing with further aspects of the subject. Certain decisions need to be made by Canadians with respect to the independent sector of the economy. In my view, governments must become more closely involved and a comprehensive program is needed, including community planning, industrial plann ng and, most important, planning oriented toward the needs of people, designed to ensure that they have an adequate opportunity to earn a decent livelihood. We cannot support the approach suggested by the task force on agriculture which, in effect, urges the government to get out of agriculture to the greatest possible extent.
The government must deoide whether it wants small businessmen, farmers and fishermen to continue to operate. If it decides in the affirmative, commitments must be made to set up programs to deal with their needs. This means a change in the attitude of the people whom we call small businessmen, farmers and fishermen. There must be greater receptivity to the prospect of change. At the same time, I wish to make it clear that I do not blame many of these people for resisting some of the proposals for change which have been made up to now, because they have been most inadequate; they have failed to deal with the problems affecting these people.
Many small businessmen, farmers and fishermen have in the past taken what they call an independent outlook. They have even espoused a free enterprise attitude in the past. However, many have found through experience, sometimes bitter experience, that it is in their best interests to work together and apply the principle of co-operation rather than the principle of competition as embodied in the "dog eat dog" philosophy in which they were trained. As I say, public programs are needed, not pro-

grams which are foisted on people from the top or from government offices but programs which are worked out in conjunction with the people directly concerned. It is only through such a process that we can make the democratic system work; it is only through such a process that we can find solutions to some of the problems facing the Canadian society.
I hope that as we deal with this bill the government will give serious consideration to the needs of these groups of people. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my speech will not be long; however, I wish to say a few words on Bill C-191, entitled "An Act to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act".
Nothing much is new in this legislation except that a limit is set on the total amount provided for loans, as shown in the explanatory notes, and I quote:
This amendment would provide for an additional three year loan period from July X, 1971 to June 30, 1974 during which guaranteed farm improvement loans may he made.
This amendment would provide that the aggregate principal amount of guaranteed farm improvement loans that may be made during the loan period ending on June 30, 1974 shall not exceed $900 million for all chartered banks and $300 million for all other lenders.
The last time the government requested the continuation of this legislation, I expressed my opinion on the loans granted for farm improvements and to small businesses. Yet farmers are still experiencing the same difficulties as before when they want to secure these loans. It seems that the government enacts legislation without asking itself whether it will benefit the interested people.
I believe that the Farm Improvement Loans Act belong to that kind of legislation at least as concerns our area. At first, when considering this legislation, we were anxious to see the results it would have among the farmers.
Seven or eight years later, in Quebec, and mainly in the Roberval area, we fail to see what good it did. It could have had many beneficial results if the government had agreed to listen to our advice and had increased somewhat the advantages offered to the farmers.
The problem in my region is first to get a loan. In fact, as I have often said to the inspectors in my region. I believe you are paid by the federal government to refuse loans and not to grant them." Everything was done to refuse a loan to a farmer who needed it. All kinds of difficulties were raised and, in certain cases, I have heard good farmers being told by the inspectors that it was

better for them to leave their farm and settle in the city rather than ask for loans.
I am not strongly in favour of loans. The more is lent to the farmers, the more they are forced to get into debt and the more they face bankruptcy. As an old farmer used to say: "With all those loans and never any direct help or protection, this is what happens. Thirty years ago I had a lot of money in the bank when I used horses to farm my land." Today, on the same farm and with the sane number of hands, we still work about 15 or 16 hours a day. Unfortunately, my three pieces of land are mortgaged and all I will bequeath to my children will be a heap of mortgages.
When all is said and done, what does the government do? They are not the lenders, but they do encourage banks and other lenders to grant loans to our farmers who get deeper and deeper into debt. Most important of all, chartered banks must not lose a cent. As for the farmer, he often has to give up his land. Many of them lost everthing but the chartered banks never lose a single cent because the government protects them.
It is difficult to have loans accepted. Inspectors are too strict and not familiar with our area. We see all kinds of nonsense. A loan was even refused because the road leading to the farmer's home was gravelled.
That is why I already quoted figures on loans granted in the western provinces and in Quebec. Everybody was astounded: 2,000 loans are granted in western Canada, only 100 or 150 in Quebec. You have the proof there of the strictness of inspectors and of the small number of loans granted in Quebec.
The second problem relates to interest rates. They will go up to 8 J per cent. Given the rates at which banks lend money nowadays, we shall still face the same problem: banks are not interested at all in lending at a rate of 8 or 81 per cent while they can grant loans elsewhere at the rate of 11 or 12 per cent.
That is why bank doors are closed to farmers and nobody can blame them. Bankers are justified in not lending to farmers when they can lend the same money at a rate of 9, 9J, 10, 10J and 11 per cent. As I always said, the law fails in that when the government determines a fixed interest to absorb the surplus payable by the farmer to have his application accepted, it should also agree to pay a discount.
You did not fail to notice the jump in number of federal loans granted in Quebec when the province decided to pay a discount as high as 3 per cent.
If the government seriously intends its loans to be of assistance to farmers with an interest rate of 8 or 8|- per cent when banks can lend at least at 11 per cent, it should be prepared to pay a 3 per cent discount or to refund this same amount to the banks or to the various lenders. Bankers would then be quite willing and ready to lend to farmers who, in turn, could acquire necessary farm implements and land.
With respect to farm machinery, we repeatedly asked the government to grant some assistance to the farmers,

because it was the purchase of such machinery which drove them into debt. As a matter of fact, this machinery costs twice as much as it should, and the farmer pays a third time for it in the form of interest. This is why today he has a mortgage on his land. Governments have never done anything to help him.
If the government will not freeze the price of farm machinery, it should at least assist farmers with grants. On the other hand, if it wants to protect the major manufacturers of farm machinery, let it grant them a 20, 25 or 30 per cent subsidy on their production cosis. This would compensate the farmer, who would not be facing bankruptcy today because of the cost of his machinery, and especially because he had to pay three times their price before owing them.
I wonder how many times we have made such a request. I am at it again tonight. We will be considering this bill and I hope the government will improve on it in such a way that farm loans will benefit farmers rather than banks and other lenders. The government could allow a discount or better still grant direct financial assistance for that purpose.
Where loans to small businesses are concerned, the problem is somewhat the same. In this respect, it has been said that according to the amending bill a further three-year period will be allowed for the granting of loans. Indeed, the explanatory notes included in the bill read as follows:
-the aggregate principal amount of guaranteed farm improvement loans that may be made during the loan period ending June 30, 1974 shall not exceed $200 milion for all chartered banks and $100 million for all other lenders.
A few loans have been granted to small businesses. The chartered banks keep their doors well closed because such loans are still more hazardous.
I could say the same about the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Because of the various interest rates the banks are absolutely not interested.
I hope that the government will have the opportunity to introduce amendments to this bill and to see to it once and for all that the people for whom those acts are enacted get more out of them.

maintopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENT PROVIDING ADDITIONAL THREE-YEAR LOAN PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-191 is an omnibus bill which seeks to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Business Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. While I have great interest in the development of our agricultural community and the small business community, I intend to deal only briefly tonight with the section of the bill which seeks to amend the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act.
This bill calls for the repeal of certain sections of the act. The first amendment would combine the two existing loan periods into one loan period in order to fully utilize the entire $20 million aggregate amount presently available for these two periods. The second amendment would provide for an additional three-year loan period from
Farm Improvement Loans Acts July 1, 1971, to June 30, 1974, during which guaranteed fisheries improvement loans may be made. It further provides that the aggregate principal amount of the guaranteed fisheries improvement loans which may be made in the new loan period shall not exceed $20 million for all chartered banks and $10 million for all other lenders.
I think it is important to remember that the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act came into force in December, 1955, for a period of three years and as a result of amendments from time to time thereafter the lending period was extended and the bill before us extends the act until June 30, 1974. It is my understanding that the intent of the legislation originally was the extension of term credit to fishermen for a variety of fishing improvement projects.
The maximum amount which may be borrowed by an individual fisherman is $25,000 and the terms of repayment are arranged so as to take account of the borrower's particular circumstances and other relevant factors, subject to the maximum term of repayment of 10 years. Maximum interest rates applicable in the year under review were 7f per cent from April 1, 1969, to September
30,	1969, and 8i per cent from October 1, 1969, to March
31,	1970. Loans must be secured, and a borrower is required to provide a reasonable portion of the cost of a purchase or project from his own resources.
A quick look at the annual report tabled for the year ending March 31, 1970, will show that fishermen since the inception of the act have not been falling over one another in order to avail themselves of the benefits provided by this legislation. In fact, from December 12, 1955, to March 31, 1970, only 3,148 loans amounting to $9,851,296 were made. The amount of losses which had to be paid by the government as a result of the guarantees in this act amounted to $13,400. Nothing could indicate more clearly to anyone the integrity of Canada's fishermen. It is to their credit that the government of this country, over a period of 15 years of loans totalling almost $10 million, was only required to pay something in the order of $13,000 in losses. I point out to you, Sir, there are very few people as a group who enjoy such an enviable credit rating.
It is also interesting to examine the number of loans and the provinces in which they were made. I shall not quote all the figures because other members of our party may wish to participate in this debate. However, it is worth while to note that since the inception of the act 15 years ago, the following loans were made in the various provinces. These are totals covering a period of 15 years. British Columbia, 1,118; Alber'a, none; Saskatchewan, 1; Manitoba, 9; Ontario, 63; Quebec, 127; New Brunswick, 175; Nova Scotia, 711; Prince Edward Island, 924 and Newfoundland, 20, for a total of 3,148 loans.
From these figures it can be clearly seen that in British Columbia the total loans amounted to more than half the loans made in the four Atlantic provinces. I hold no brief for the fact that British Columbia fishermen obviously made greater use of the act than the fishermen in Atlan-

December 1, 1970
Farm Improvement Loans Acts tic Canada, but I submit that there must be a reason for this. I suggest it is because our area of Canada has been suffering acute disparity for so many years that our citizens, and especially our fishermen, are loth to assume heavy debts at the high interest rates which, as I have indicated, have been charged by this government.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Quite frankly, I believe the time has arrived for a complete review by the government of its policy in so far as our fishermen are concerned. For example, I personally do not believe that the present shipbuilding subsidy program is adequate. A subsidy of 35 per cent is inadequate at the present time, in light of present day costs. It is true that fishermen from the Atlantic provinces and Quebec can obtain loans from their respective fishermen loans boards for the purchase of new vessels, new power units and certain types of fishing gear. However, due to the high cost of construction and the increased cost of fishing gear and equipment, east coast fishermen engaged in the production of a low-cost variety of fish, operating on a shorter limited season cannot, even with the availability of provincial loans, meet the high cost of fishing boats or look after their replacement.
Surely the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) must recognize that the construction subsidies on such vessels established some years ago should not have been cut back to 35 per cent. I would be the first to agree that subsidies on new draggers or trawlers, whether of wood or steel construction, need to be controlled and a stated amount should be available for each fiscal year. However, the abolition of the subsidy and then its reinstatement at the 35 per cent level has proved disastrous to the fishing industry and to our shipbuilding industry.
In view of the high unemployment rate in Atlantic Canada, I wonder why greater emphasis has not been placed by this government on a suitable over-all program of assistance to our fishermen in the form of aids to shipbuilding. Any funds extended in this manner would provide much needed employment in our shipyards, while adding to our commercial and fishing fleets. Without a shipbuilding subsidy our shipbuilders cannot hope to compete with foreign builders, a fact which was recognized by the recent 17 per cent export subsidy on ships announced only this week by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin).
We cannot compete due to our high labour costs and high cost of materials. I submit that our present high rates of taxation have not been helpful to our fishermen or our shipbuilders. At the present time shipbuilding in my constituency is at an all-time low, with only one or two small longliners under construction. However, this does not mean that more ships are not required, because more fishing vessels are needed as our present ships become obsolete. At the present time there is a need for new scallop draggers, and ships are required for the queen crab industry. With the expanded demand for fisheries products of all types in the United States, new groundfish draggers also must be constructed, ships which are capable of conversion to new and different
methods of fishing, ships which can range great distances, ships which can fish deeper waters.
However, I point out to you, Sir, that unless the government recognizes its responsibility to our shipbuilding industry and to our fishermen by establishing a more realistic shipbuilding policy, the ships presently required by Canadians will be built in foreign lands. This would, of course, only aggravate our present serious unemployment problem. When a ship is built in a foreign land, it does nothing for the shipbuilding industry in Canada. It does not contain any wood or steel supplied by Canadians, it does not contain any Canadian heating equipment, any electronic equipment, any pipes or any plumbing, and the paint on its hull is not manufactured by Canadians. I know of no industry in Canada which makes a greater impact on our over-all economy than the shipbuilding industry. When a ship is constructed, it needs heat, light and power and a multitude of materials right down to the medicine chest for the sick or disabled fisherman.
For these reasons I believe the present subsidy program, rather than being helpful may in fact be harmful to our fishermen. With only a 35 per cent subsidy available, fishermen may well decide to build a ship much smaller than they require, simply because they have insufficient funds to build a ship of the size required for year-round fishing in the north Atlantic. For example, a 65-foot ship, whether it be a scallop dragger, longliner or purse seiner-whatever its purpose-simply cannot operate in the north Atlantic during the months of November, December, January, February and even part of March. If they do try to carry out fishing operations during this period, there is a physical hazard to the crew which would not be present on a larger ship.
In other words, this government, by its present policy of assisting the shipbuilding industry and assisting fishermen in providing a 35 per cent subsidy, is still encouraging short-range fishing operations at a time when all the signs are pointing to the need for long-range operations if we are to provide steady, year-round employment in the industry at stable rates of income for our fishermen. In my opinion, the 35 per cent subsidy could be increased to 50 per cent in order to offset the high cost of Canadian ship construction. This action would encourage, at the same time, more fishermen to participate in deep sea fishery, thereby increasing employment opportunities in many ancillary industries in Atlantic Canada.
As the minister is aware, extensive overfishing by foreign countries on our offshore banks is making it extremely difficult for many of our inshore fishermen to survive. We must, therefore, not only assist the inshore fishermen in acquiring the proper equipment with which to carry out their hazardous occupation, but we must do this in a manner that will make them competitive with foreign fishermen while at the same time enabling them to earn a livelihood and to provide for their families.
One way in which we can assist inshore fishermen, and for that matter deep sea fishermen as well, is by helping them cut their costs. We could move in this direction by lowering the cost of many ships that may be constructed.

December 1, 1970

On December 11, 1969, the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry announced changes in the fishing vessel insurance plan. I will not quote from this announcement. I refer to it only by date so as to remind the minister of the time he made this announcement.
I would suggest that this plan, with which I agree, be expanded. At present, for example, when a new ship is under construction it is necessary for the shipbuilder to place builder's risk insurance on the hull. Some three years ago builder's risk cost the builder .25 per cent. Today this cost, like every other, has increased and it is in the vicinity of .75 per cent. This is an increase of 300 per cent in the cost of builder's risk insurance. This cost must be integrated into the cost of the ship prior to the placing of the contract by the fisherman. The Minister of Fisheries and Forestry in his announcement of December 11, 1969, made changes in regard to the insurance which may be taken out by a fisherman or a group of fishermen on the hull after they take delivery of the ship and it is put into operation on the high seas.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Without reading the whole of the announcement, Mr. Speaker, the minister indicated that a 4 per cent rate on appraised value over $25,000 would be charged to a fisherman or group of fishermen as the price for insurance under the fishing vessel insurance plan. I would suggest that the minister take this plan one step further by incorporating in it the possibility of carrying the insurance that is required when a hull is under construction. This may sound like a small saving, but in view of the cost of ships today it may well amount to something like $600 to $800 for a fisherman or a group of fishermen if the present plan were expanded and the rate charged by the government were, say, approximately .25 per cent, the rate which was in existence some three years ago.
I would also point out that this coverage is generally placed overseas with an insurance corporation. Certainly it is not placed in Canada. Therefore, since we are subsidizing these ships, and even though I feel the 35 per cent subsidy is inadequate-it is still a part subsidy-in effect we are sending our tax dollars overseas in order to provide protection on a hull during its construction in Canada. This does not appear to me to make good sense. If we are going to assist our fishermen, I submit this is one field of endeavour that we should investigate. In effect, the government of Canada would be taking very little risk if it followed the course I propose.
I know of no instance in my native province of Nova Scotia where a ship under construction has caught fire, since the builders are very much interested in protecting their own livelihood. So, Mr. Speaker, I throw this suggestion out to the minister in the hope that he and his officials will give it some thought. In the event that they should decide to follow my earlier suggestion and expand the subsidy program to 50 per cent of the approved cost of the ship, I feel certain this would add impetus to shipbuilding in Nova Scotia, in Atlantic Canada and in fact throughout all of Canada. Also, the additional insurance program which I have suggested would be helpful in keeping down costs.

Mr. Speaker, as other hon. members have outlined, this is primarily a housekeeping bill to update the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. With respect to small business loans, I notice that it will be guaranteeing another $300 million over the next three years which, broken down, means $100 million a year. In the Farm Improvement Loans area there are guarantees that run to approximately $400 million a year. But, Mr. Speaker, we find that last year with respect to small business loans we used only a shade over $6 million of the $100 million guaranteed. If my memory serves me correctly, in the farm improvement loans area we only used something like $48 million of the $400 million guaranteed.
With all the bankruptcies prevalent and the apparent need for money in this country, one must ask why we are not using a far higher percentage of the money that is available. I submit the main reason is that the rate of interest is too high. It is totally unrealistic compared with the returns that businesses are making today. Under this legislation money can be borrowed at 8 per cent or 9 per cent, but frequently businesses make a profit of less than half of that or none at all. I support the previous speaker in saying that the taxes we have to pay today are no help, either. More encouragement should be given to the banks to overcome the time lag in the lowering of interest rates. The other day I read that somebody had said a banker is like a fellow who lends you an umbrella when the sun is shining but wants it back once it starts to rain. This is too often the case.
One of the main problems facing business today is posed by cheap imports. This will be a continuing problem and may eventually prove disastrous. I am sure nobody wants this country to become isolated in terms of trade and I can think of no better way to meet foreign competition, and at the same time combat the problem of unemployment, than getting money into the hands of small businesses. But we cannot do this unless we are willing to provide the means to lower interest rates. Several years ago when the interest rate was 5 per cent, money could be borrowed, business could be promoted and things could move ahead. But money lent under the terms now stipulated will serve no useful purpose. I suggest that the government is not really guaranteeing too much of anything because there is no demand for money at such high interest rates.
In this regard the banks are in a very favoured position. They lend the money, collect their profit through the interest on it and the government guarantees them against loss. This is a highly undersirable situation, considering the state of business today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to add just a few words to the remarks of my colleague from Nova Scotia who presented statistics on the various loan bills before us in an effort to indicate to the Parliamentary Secretary and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) some of the weaknesses of this legislation. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will be as receptive to my remarks as was his predecessor who worked with me for about a year in an effort to improve the legislation. That gentleman is in the House at the moment, and in all sincerity I must say that in the past year and a half he worked diligently to iron out the inadequacies of the legislation before us.
Perhaps we should first look at the problem, Mr. Speaker. With regard to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, as soon as one looks at the distribution of the funds to the various provinces it is obvious that something is wrong. For example, in the year ended March 31, 1969, $7,272,291 were paid for a grand total of 2,788 loans across Canada. Eighteen of these loans were made in the biggest fishing province in Canada in terms of the number of people involved.
Under the Small Businesses Loans Act for the period October to December, 1969, 306 loans were made for a grand total of $3,589,097. Five of these loans were made in the province of Prince Edward Island. In my province for that quarter there were no loans, and this year to date there have been two loans out of a total of 1,452 for the whole country. We had only two loans, when over $16 million were expended in Canada under the Small Businesses Loans Act.
That is the situation, Mr. Speaker. Now, what is the problem? The simple problem is that the government lost control of the legislation when it gave jurisdiction to the banks. It told the banks they could lend money under these acts if the applicant had a very good reason for borrowing. It was the intention of the government to assure the banks that if the individual ran into d fficulty on his repayments, the government would guarantee repayment. But the bankers are pretty shrewed and they said to the small businessman, the fisherman and, I presume, to the farmer, "We can lend you money at a much higher interest rate and not worry about this type of loan at all." That is what they have done. They have literally gone against the federal government and said, "We are not going to toe your line. We are not going to lend money to these people under this legislation."
I have come across a case which concerns me. I shall give the Parliamentary Secretary details of it afterwards, if he wishes. A man from Moreton's Harbour, a famous fishing community in Newfoundland, gave me his name, the name of the bank, the name of the bank manager and all the statistics involved. He applied for a loan under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act and the bank asked for some guarantee that he qualified.
The banks say that a person must have the capitalization behind him and they are very rigid in this regard. This was not the intention of the government at all. They intended this legislation to be of benefit to the man who was an average risk, the person who might otherwise have difficulty getting a loan. But the bank said to this applicant that they had to be sure he was a good risk, and would not give him a loan under the act. At that time there was more money in his bank account at that bank, but he did not want to touch it because it was for a rainy day. Having refused him a loan under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, the bank proceeded to grant him a loan under their general loan procedures at about 12 per cent, compared with the 7 per cent it would have cost under the act. In other words, Mr. Speaker, because of the tight money situation the banks know they can lend whatever money they have available. Consequently, in provinces where money is tight, provinces with the greatest regional disparity, the banks are not interested in lending money under this legislation.
Last year I raised the question with the then Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance. He wrote to the president of the Canadian Bankers' Association, who replied as to why he felt money was not being advanced under the act. I know that the department applied pressure to try and loosen up financing, but they have not been successful because the banks have control. I say, Mr. Speaker, that this legislation is a waste of time.
We can do one of three things. We can take the legislation and toss it in the wastepaper basket, which may be the best thing to do with it; we can pass it, even though it is not functioning properly; or we can try to gain control of the lending taking place under it and bring the legislation back for further amendment. Let the federal government set up its own funding agency, if that is necessary and possible. I do not know whether that is a worth-while suggestion. It seems to be reasonable.
