[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
If the federal government is to become involved in assisting small businessmen, whether they be farmers, fishermen or other small businessmen, it should try to acquire control over its own legislation. Under present arrangements the people involved are not given a fair deal, especially in areas where there is a high degree of regional disparity. This is the problem. I have presented this case to the Minister of Finance on a number of occasions. He understands it. He is a very capable minister and understands the problem of regional disparity. He understands that fiscal and monetary policies must be uniformly applied across the nation.
This legislation is a perfect example of what I mean. We ought to make special legislative or regulatory arrangements to govern banks in areas where money is tightest. Those arrangements should govern the bank managers or the lending institutions concerned. We have laid down regulations governing their behaviour in the past and we shall have to adapt our policies to take care of areas such as the Atlantic region. I do not doubt that these remarks apply also to Quebec and some parts of western Canada; they apply to all regions where unemployment is very high.
We see these difficulties every time there is tight money. We see them especially in areas most affected by tight money, areas such as the Atlantic provinces and the slow-growth areas. I am concerned about this. Something is radically wrong. Small businessmen have made representations to me on the subject. Some of them have gone to banks, asked for loans and have been refused loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act, yet they have been offered loans at the regular interest rates by the banks. Obviously, this is a violation of the intention of the legislation passed by the federal government. It shows that the banks are really saying to the government, "You can keep your money and your guarantees. We are not interested, because we can lend to other industries at higher rates of interest." That is why I say this piece of legislation will be a complete waste of time unless we amend it so as to give us greater control over its application.
My only other point is this. Let us consider the fishing industry on the Atlantic coast. I am not too familiar with the industry on the Pacific coast, but perhaps the same considerations obtain there. Many of our fishermen are caught in a squeeze. They are inshore fishermen and they need to become fishermen in a bigger way. They need the capability to go where the fish are and to catch them. These men are caught in a squeeze. Not many years ago we had about 10,000 inshore fishermen in my province. I could not quote statistics for the other provinces. They were men who operated with small boats, some of them 35 feet long and less, with inadequate equipment and inadequate technology. These are the men who made up the bulk of our traditional Atlantic fishery.
These people are now faced with this situation. The inshore fishery stock having been depleted by the fishing vessels of the Soviet Union and the East Germans, our
Farm Improvement Loans Acts inshore fishermen cannot get out to where the fish are. The fish are no longer as close inshore as they were, and if these men are to make a living from the fishery they must acquire the capability of going farther out to sea. These traditional inshore fishermen need better fishing gear. They are still good fishermen; they know more about fishing than any of us. They are professionals, and they are caught in the squeeze. They cannot go after the fish. They need larger boats and better electronic equipment. They need radar and sonar, better nets and the technology that will enable them to go out where the fish are and find them.
I do not know how many thousands of fishermen in Atlantic Canada today-and there are roughly 10,000 in my province-cannot earn a living with the fishing equipment they possess. I say that the Department of Fisheries and the Department of Finance ought to get together and try to come up with an over-all, comprehensive program which will help these people. The alternative for these men is help under the Canada Assistance Plan, which they do not want. Fishermen do not want that. They are capable of earning their own living. They are people with skills and trades and able to prosecute a fishery in a reasonable manner.
Some of them have been kept afloat with the longliner program. Not long ago the government introduced a program under which, to help the fishery in one province, 60 longliners were built. That program is relatively small when one realizes that there are roughly 1,000 communities in one Atlantic province alone which need help. Sixty longliners do not go far among 1,000 communities. There are roughly 20,000 fishermen in one province. The government should seriously consider a comprehensive program along the lines recommended by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse). Under it the fishermen would have access to improved technology, which would assist them in their fishery and help them out of the squeeze.
I become depressed when I see such people in my riding. During the past week-end I talked to 300 people in a community on Fogo Island and every second man I talked to did not have the technological ability to get out to where the fish are. Yet these men are eager to fish, and given half a chance they would do a good job. I should like to describe some of the things I saw, but perhaps hon. members might not wish to hear me speak for half an hour about the heartbreaking cases of these people who want nothing but the chance to use their skills.
I shall give one more example of what I mean, Mr. Speaker. I met a man from a community called Seldom. He has a small boat; it is 40 or 43 feet long. Nobody, but nobody in the fishery stands a substantial chance in a small boat because you have to go a long way offshore to fish. That man has been going 25 miles offshore into the Atlantic. He leaves the shore and he goes straight out in the Atlantic. First of all, his facilities for getting back are inadequate. I hope to make representations to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) for the installation of better equipment to help people like him get back to shore.
December 1, 1970

Farm Improvement Loans Acts That man has no radar and no sonar. He cannot sound the bottom and know what is beneath him. The Russians are out there with enough technology to frighten the hair off your scalp. Yet he is out there in a 43-foot boat and he has with him about five men.
This individual came to me and said, "I am ashamed. I am only landing between 4,000 and 5,000 pounds of fish, whereas I should be landing 15,000 and 20,000 pounds a day. But I cannot do it." He has to go between 25 or 30 miles offshore, where the big boats go, and he does not have sufficient electronic equipment. I said to him, "Can't you go to the provincial fisheries loan board?" He said, "But the loan board will ask, what security do you have?" This is a provincial board which makes loans.
Several people in the community have told me that he is one of the most reputable small businessmen in the community. If given the chance, he would be capable of bringing in two or three times the amount of fish that he brings in at the moment. He is capable of providing five families at least with a livelihood, and there are another ten families who work on shore in association with his venture. So about 15 families make a living from the capabilities of one man. How much money does he want to buy the equipment he needs? He needs $5,000. That is how much he needs to be able to go out where the fish are. If he does not get it he will have to go on welfare; he has no other choice. I could describe dozens of cases such as that, cases involving capable people who need boats of 50, 60 or 70 feet if they are to go out to the fish.
The hon. member for South Shore said that these men need the benefits of advanced technology to enable them to get out into the Atlantic. When you talk about those waters, you are talking about big boats, but I have been talking about the small, inshore fishermen, some of whom in their small boats have to go out between 25 and 30 miles. These men would bring back more fish if they had the necessary equipment. On the same evening I have been talking about, one fishing craft in the community brought back 33,000 pounds of fish worth $1,650. I think it had a five-man crew. They obtained that catch because they had the necessary radar and sonar equipment. They could find the fish and they knew what type of seabottom was under them. However, I am not going to draw any more maps. It is important for us to take a very close look at this legislation, because it is not serving our purposes in Atlantic Canada. The banks, with their loan policies, have deliberately frustrated the efforts of the federal government in the implementation of this program.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
My second point is that we must have a better scheme to help fishermen and small businessmen. The resources are there and these men should be able to reap them. A comprehensive program should be established so that our fishermen cannot only earn a living but can make a significant contribution to Canada. The alternative is the Canada Assistance Plan.

maintopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENT PROVIDING ADDITIONAL THREE-YEAR LOAN PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members listened with great interest to the speech of
the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundri-gan). It brought back memories of the time his party formed the government. Similar speeches, including some by Liberals, were made at that time and fell on deaf ears. His party formed the government in office and should have used their influence to solve these problems. We are involved in thinking in terms of the political philosophy of the government in an aspect of the so-called free enterprise or capitalist economy.
The manner in which the bill is constructed indicates that the government does not honestly believe in its own philosophy with regard to the free enterprise system. The government believes in foreign-controlled enterprise, a monopoly kind of enterprise with price-fixing conspiracies and the like. Even in those terms a person with initiative and drive is probably exemplified by small businessmen, fishermen and farmers.
Farmers and fishermen are our primary producers of food-stuffs, the farmer more than the fisherman because there is an element of union organization among fishermen which gives them economic leverage. The farmer has no authority, control or say over the price he pays for the machinery and equipment that he buys, or the price he receives for the goods he sells. The fisherman is in that position to a slightly lesser extent. These two groups of primary producers are at the mercy of an element in society that has control over some aspect of our economy, whether it be a manufacturer of equipment or gear or a distributor of foodstuffs.
By this legislation and the three acts that have been brought into force, the government has attempted to equate the prime producer and small businessman with large business. There is an attempt to force small businessmen, farmers and fishermen who do not have control over their economic destiny into an uncompetitive position with regard to the money market. As pointed out by the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate, he is forced to deal from an unfair advantage position with the private chartered banks. He is forced to compete with the large fishing companies which by reason of their corporate structure can quite easily borrow money from the banks or float debentures at higher interest rates in order to obtain capital. Fishermen are at the mercy of the banks which may not want to lend them money, depending on the current interest rate.
The proposals in the white paper on taxation in so far as tax measures are concerned attempt to equate small businessmen with large business concerns. They should not be subject to equation. The intent and purpose of Parliament should be to give some advantage to our primary producers. Public funds should be available for loans at a rate that is reasonable, not usurious. The facilities of the nation should be provided within the concept of an extremely large credit union which would provide a service to our primary producers rather than drive them into a poorer and poorer economic situation.
I wish to refer briefly to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act and the annual report which was published in March this year. The report paraphrases this act. It points out that under the Fisheries Improvement Loans

Act money may be borrowed from a bank for the purpose of buying and building fishing vessels, acquiring fishing equipment, major repair or overhaul of fishing vessels, purchase or construction of shore installations, construction, repair or alteration of buildings required by a primary fishing enterprise, or other prescribed developments of or improvements to primary fishing enterprises. There is a limit of $25,000 on the amount an individual fisherman may borrow.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-INCLUSION OF HOSPITAL WORKERS-PAYMENT OF COST
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-INCLUSION OF HOSPITAL WORKERS-PAYMENT OF COST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 25 I raised the question in the House as to whether hospital workers should be included in the unemployment insurance plan. If they were, then the federal and provincial governments should costshare this program. There were several reasons for raising this subject. In 1951, Hon. Paul Martin, then Minister of National Health and Welfare, ruled that they should not be because there were few layoffs of hospital workers: attrition and retirement look after this matter; this is the way hospital workers leave the job. He therefore felt it would be an unnecessary cost to the hospital system.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
Every minister of health since that time has come to the same conclusion. Surely they cannot all be wrong. But if they have been wrong and unemployment insurance is necessary, it is my contention that the federal government and the provincial government concerned should pay the contributions under a cost-sharing program. I take this view because the federal government has said: You must limit increases in total costs to 8J per cent. Provincial governments have said the same thing, in spite of the fact that hospital costs have been rising at around 15 per cent.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
According to the government, the increase must not amount to more than 8J per cent, without provision for new facilities needed to keep operations up-to-date. And we must remember that this is an age in which new diagnostic methods are being introduced at tremendous speed, adding extra costs every year, an age in which our knowledge of medical and scientific facts is doubling every eight years. Costs will continue to increase if we are to provide top quality medical care. Otherwise, research will be stifled and medical progress will be retarded.
The government well knows that salary increases have amounted to more than 10 per cent across Canada and that 70 per cent of a hospital's budget goes in salaries. Yet it proposes to take 2 per cent out of the 8J per cent I have mentioned and still expects the hospitals to meet their commitments. In effect, we are asked to run our hospitals on the basis of a 64 per cent increase in total costs even though the real cost is twice that amount. Unless salaries are increased, this action will take $174 million out of the workers' pockets and another $174 million out of hospital budgets.
A hospital has only a limited budget, and costs have to be met. If it becomes necessary to raise salaries, the size of staffs will have to be cut. No one will argue that the workers do not need an increase in pay, bearing in mind today's spiralling costs. What happens if administrators have to let people go? There is very little fat in hospital budgets today and if anyone is let out, a nurse or a helper, the quality of the service goes down. When the nursing staff is affected, patients suffer directly.
Kenneth Box, administrator of the Queensway Hospital, Toronto, said he feels that if the 84 per cent guideline must be followed he will have to cut 40 of the employees from a staff of 700 workers in a 350-bed hospital. Douglas Sneddon, executive director of the Sick Children's Hospital in Toronto says he is in trouble if he wants to live up to his responsibilities and pay a fair wage to the 3,000 employees. I think this makes the point. There must be no cutting of essential services in hospital care and no reduction in the quality of care. The government has promised this, but one becomes leery of government promises. When they brought in medicare they set up a health research fund to train the necessary doctors according to the ground rules. Then, when the centres were under construction, right in the middle of it they said: We are hard up; we must cut the fund.
Mr. Speaker, I have just come from a committee meeting in which we were talking about this very question. If unemployment insurance is necessary for hospital workers, if it is necessary to keep cost increases to 8J per cent, then the federal government and the provincial governments, in all fairness to the people of Canada and to hospital workers, ought to pay for it on a cost-sharing basis.

maintopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-IMPLEMENTATION OF LAND USE REGULATIONS-PERFORMANCE BONDS
NORTHERN AFFAIRS-IMPLEMENTATION OF LAND USE REGULATIONS-PERFORMANCE BONDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 24 I asked the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) when the regulations respecting land use operations in the ftikon
and Northwest Territories would come into effect. The following supplementary question was also asked:
In view of the required posting of $100,000 performance bonds by the two oil companies doing work on Banks Island in the Arctic, why has this regulation not been applied to all companies doing similar work in the Arctic area?
The minister indicated that the land use requirements would soon become legal, but I received no answer to the supplementary question. I find it difficult to understand why the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has been so long in bringing down the northern land use regulations. I understand the department has been working on these regulations for almost two years. The legislation to which they will apply was passed many months ago, but the greatest tragedy of all is that a great and increasing economic development is taking place in northern Canada with no effective regulations to guide it. This is a shameful situation and one that should not be allowed.
It is obvious that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development places low priority on the protection of our northern environment. It seems that the whole department is bogged down as far as environmental protection is concerned. The lengthy delay in instituting the northern land use regulations indicates this. I understand that the original draft dealing with these land use regulations has been drastically revised. The chances are that when the new draft comes to light we will find that the exploiters of our northern resources have forced the government to do away with some of the most effective control regulations. I will not speculate as to what we will find in the regulations when they are brought down by the minister, but I suggest there should be no further delay in having the regulations announced and in bringing the vast amount of exploration in our Canadian north under some type of control.
In checking over the budget for the department I feel that it is far too low if any major effort is to be made to enforce the regulations and to keep inspectors in the area. An adequate staff must be found, trained and hired. There is no indication that the department has proceeded at any great speed in this connection. Perhaps the minister could inform us how large a staff is already on hand to do the job of inspection once the regulations are announced.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Another major problem in connection with the whole northern development program is that there appear to be no overriding central objectives set out by the department. Long-term objectives are desperately needed for the north. We must know how the residents and the wildlife fit into the exploration and economic programs which will flow from it. This matter should be given the highest priority because the residents of the north will be living there long after the oil and the mineral resources have become exhausted.
I requested information from the minister concerning the reason other companies working in our northern areas were not bonded as those on Banks Island had
[Mr. Perrault.l
December 1, 1970

been. Perhaps he can give me that information tonight. Is the bonding of companies engaged in exploration work in the north one of the new regulations to be brought down by the minister? If so, does it cover the entire area, or is the bonding of companies to apply only to certain sections of our Arctic areas? It would seem to me that immense ecological damage could be done by any company and that bonding is an excellent method by which to make certain that companies engaged in this exploratory work live up to the regulations. This is especially essential in our northern areas where the ecology is so fragile that it can be easily destroyed for centuries to come.
During the debates in this House on legislation dealing with our great north country there was agreement that our northern ecology must be protected at all costs. The need for land use permits with tough regulations was pointed out. The need for sharply increased research into Arctic problems was another requirement. It was also urged that the rate of exploration and exploitation should be slowed until we had the regulations to control it, as well as the research background and experimentation upon which to base our decisions and a fully trained staff to enforce the conditions under which land use permits are issued.
I urge the minister to bring down these regulations without further delay. I trust he has not given in to the economic interests in the north and so watered down these regulations that they will be largely ineffective. Land use permits are especially powerful weapons with which to protect our environment, and they must cover the entire area. Perhaps the minister can assure the House on this point tonight.
There is already a great deal of information available on our Canadian north. This must be drawn together and properly evaluated. I trust the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has already started to do this. I hope it has drawn heavily on the expertise to be found in other government departments such as Energy, Mines and Resources, and on the experience of other countries.
In closing, I again express my disappointment at the failure of the department to bring down long before now the northern land use regulations which are so vital to the protection of our northern ecology. I hope the minister can tell us tonight why there has been such a lengthy
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
delay in setting up these regulations and when he expects to introduce them to the House.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out to the hon. member that his concern is rather surprising since, in the last few months, this House has passed three different acts to ensure a more rational development of the North, and so that the mistakes made in the South might not be repeated up there.
The hon. member will surely remember the will I myself introduced on the protection of the Arctic waters, as well as the bill dealing with the conservation of the inland waters in the Yukon and Northwest Territories which represent almost a sixth of all fresh waters in the world. To my mind, that act is the most modern there is.
In addition, one must also remember the measure passed at the end of the last session, authorizing the minister to enact stricter regulations respecting resource development in the Northwest Territories.
However, we cannot formulate the regulations mentioned by the hon. member before legislation is passed. I hope the regulations will soon be approved by the cabinet. Meanwhile, I myself have taken the initiative to oblige industries in areas where we feel the ecological balance is at stake, where native populations continue to live on fishing and hunting, to put up $100,000 to prove their good faith.
I must say that on Banks Island, the companies involved as well as the Eskimos and department officials have been working hand in hand and that the new procedure makes it possible for everybody to co-operate. Otherwise the department would be working alone, while the companies and the inhabitants of the Arctic Islands or other northern areas would be working on their side. Indeed, we are trying to co-ordinate the efforts of all those interested in convervation and exploration.
I think that the hon. member would be pleased to know that we will soon be enacting the regulations which he has been anticipating, but in the meantime, we have obtained the full co-operation of the companies involved as well as that of the native people.

speechtext:
STATEMENT ON CONSULTATIONS IN LONDON, BRUSSELS AND GENEVA RE: E.E.C. ENLARGEMENT
On behalf of the Government and accompanied by officials of the Departments of External Affairs, Finance, Agriculture, and Indsutry, Trade and Commerce, I visited Geneva, London and Brussels in October to put forward Canadian interests in the current negotiations for enlargement of the European Economic Community.
In Gevena, I had a tour d'horizon of current world trade issues with the Director-General of the GATT. In London, I met with Prime Minister Heath and three of his Cabinet colleagues. I had talks in Brussels with five of the eight members of the E.E.C. Commission, the permanent representatives of the six member states, the British negotiating team, the Ambassadors of the other applicant countries (Ireland, Denmark and Norway) and the Ambassadors of the United States, Australia and New Zealand.
Those with whom I met welcomed our representations-they clearly wanted to have a better understanding of Canada's point of view.
Main Themes
In my conversations, I highlighted four main themes:
1.	Our concerns about the negative effects of E.E.C. enlargement on Canada's access to the markets of the United Kongdom and Western Europe and its repercussions on the framework and patterns of world trade.
2.	Our conviction that in some instances mutuality of interests exists between Canada and Britain and the E.E.C., offering scope for adjustments.
3.	Our intention to bring into play at an appropriate stage the contractual rights and obligations, under bilateral arrangements and under the GATT, which would be affected by E.E.C. enlargement.
4.	Our views as to the importance of developing new initiatives for freeing of trade on a multilateral basis during the period of European negotiations.
Some Effects of Enlargement
In discussing the direct impact E.E.C. enlargement would have on Canadian trade, I drew a statistical picture of the changes in access terms which our exports to Britain would face if that country adopted the E.E.C. Common External Tariff and the Common Agricultural Policy unchanged. Only about 36 per cent of these exports would continue to receive free entry compared with some 94 per cent at present. The remainder would face tariffs, loss of Commonwealth preferences and reverse preferences in favour of our E.E.C. competitors. Our agricultural exports would be in an even more difficult position as the inward-looking Common Agricultural Policy makes use of levies, subsidies and other special protective devices.
The actual effects on the volume and profitability of Canadian sales would, of course, vary considerably from one item to another. However, it was important to ensure that the parties to the negotiations were fully seized of the fact that almost 70 per cent of our exports to Britain
would be adversely affected under the present Common External Tariff and Common Agricultural Policy.
I underlined that Britain is Canada's second largest export market accounting for about one-quarter of our overseas sales. It has been purchasing more than $1 billion of Canadian goods annually in recent years and in 1970, its purchases will exceed this level by a considerable margin. Our exports to the E.E.C. and other applicant countries are approximately of the same magnitude as our sales to Britain. Some of these would also be adversely affected by E.E.C. enlargement.
As regards the more general implications, we emphasized the danger of a polarization of the world trading community into inward-looking rival blocks. The E.E.C. is already the world's largest trading entity. Enlarged, it would account for more than one-quarter of world trade, that is, not including intra-Community trade-compared with about 20 per cent for the United States. About 50 of the 91 members of the GATT could be either members of the E.E.C. or countries associated with it.
I urged that the E.E.C. use its influence to facilitate and encourage continued expansion of trade on a worldwide basis and not only within its own grouping of member and associated countries. The world trading community and the E.E.C. itself would have much to gain from such an outward-looking policy. On the other hand, if E.E.C. enlargement mainly has the effect of limiting and diverting trade from third countries, the Community is itself bound to lose over the longer run in terms of consumer and producer costs. Moreover, outside suppliers could not remain indifferent to the loss of important traditional markets for their goods in the E.E.C. and in the countries associated with it.
The Enlargement Negotiations and Canada
As honourable members are aware, Britain has already told the E.E.C. that it is prepared in principle to accept the Common External Tariff and the Common Agricultural Policy.
As regards accommodation for outside interests, the only specific issues Britain has raised in the negotiations relate to access for New Zealand butter and lamb and Commonwealth sugar and to relationships between Commonwealth developing countries and the enlarged community.
Certain arrangements which Britain is seeking in its own interest could help some of our exports. For example, as I have already told the House, nine of the twelve industrial materials for which Britain has requested special arrangements are of interest to Canada. These are aluminum, lead, zinc, newsprint, wood pulp, plywood, phosphorus, ferro-silicon and silicon carbide. Together they account for more than one-fifth of our sales in the British market.
There would also be, in case of enlargement of the E.E.C., a transitional period during which Canadian exporters could adjust to the new situation. The British have proposed that the application of the common tariff
December 1, 1970

on industrial goods be staged over three years and that there should be a transitional period of six years for agriculture.
On the basis of my discussions with European leaders, I can say that Britain and the E.E.C. are prepared to explore with us areas where their interests may to some extent coincide with our own. They are also willing to maintain a two-way flow of views and information with Canada throughout the negotiations. We hope that their agenda will not be too rigid to allow them to do these things in a meaningful way.
It would, however, be misleading for me to suggest that there is prospect of any major accommodation of Canadian trade interests in the short term. Apart from whatever possibilities may exist for adjustments based on mutuality of interests, we must assume that, if the negotiations succeed, Canadian exports to Britain will eventually be subject to a Common External Tariff and a Common Agricultural Policy.
The general situation as far as access for Canadian goods is concerned would be significantly improved if the trading countries of the world undertook, during the enlargement negotiations or before the end of the transitional period, a broad negotiation to reduce tariffs and non-tariff barriers to trade. This would mitigate the trade diverting effects of E.E.C. enlargement in much the same way as the Dillon and Kennedy Rounds eased the impact on third countries of the original formation of the E.E.C.
For the present, however, European energies are being concentrated on the re-shaping of Europe. In Brussels, it was emphasized that "elargissement" is only one of the current preoccupations of the E.E.C.-the other being "approfondissement," the progressive transformation of the Community from a customs union into a full economic and monetary union. We suggested that they should give more thought to the need for a "modialisation"-or adaptation of the results of the enlargement negotiations to the requirements of world trade.
European Views
In both Brussels and London, there was a tendency to agree that the Canadians were exaggerating the impact of E.E.C. enlargement on their trade. I was told that many of our exports would benefit from the dynamics of growth of the enlarged Community and its rapidly expanding import needs. Reference was made to the fact that the E.E.C.'s imports have more than doubled since 1958 when the Community came into being. It was also pointed out that the average level of the Common External Tariff on industrial goods was lower than that of the United States. Other favourable factors, including intercompany arrangements, could, some Europeans believe, ensure continued exports to an enlarged Community of some of our industrial goods.
In our meetings in London, the British sought to convince us that there would always be a large market for Canadian hard wheat in Britain because it was needed to maintain the right balance in milling operations.
We were repeatedly assured by all that the policy of the E.E.C. (and perhaps even more so of an enlarged E.E.C.) would be responsible and outward-looking. In
fact, all said Europe "would not be comfortable with an inward-looking orientation."
We listened carefully to these reassuring assertions. I said we sincerely hoped that events would bear out the assumption of faster European economic growth following enlargement. This would not help us however, we emphasized, in those cases where their tariffs or other trade barriers were highly restrictive, as in the agricultural sector.
If Europeans are going to continue to need our industrial materials to sustain efficient economic growth, why impose on themselves the burden of paying significant customs duties on some of these products? If the enlarged Community will continue to need our wheat, should not the relevant regulations of the Common Agricultural Policy be adjusted to facilitate such trade.
I welcome their predictions that an enlarged Community would be outward-looking and said that we hoped to see this reflected in the progress of the GATT work program and in future initiatives toward trade liberalization.
Canadian Strategy
What will be the Canadian attitude in the months and years to come? We shall continue, as I indicated, to keep considerations of this kind before our trading partners in Europe throughout the negotiations. We shall continue to seek areas of mutuality of interests. We shall continue to urge the E.E.C. and the applicant countries, when they are weighing the merits of alternative solutions, to include in the balance the interests of third countries and the future of the world trading community.
As honourable members know, my colleague, Mr. Sharp, is now in Europe and will be discussing the implications of E.E.C. enlargement for broad Canada-Europe relations.
Our discussions will be pursued in the coming months with all present and prospective members of the Community. In our consultations with them, we are placing considerable emphasis on the kind of relationship which an enlarged Community would have with Canada and other countries and trading groups.
As the negotiations in Europe proceed, we shall be considering how our important contractual rights and obligations can be put into play most effectively. We shall also be reviewing the implications of E.E.C. enlargement for Britain's preferential access to the Canadian market.
In the meantime, we shall use our influence in the GATT to maintain the momentum of trade liberalization efforts and press in particular for a major round of negotiations before the results of the enlargement negotiations are put into effect. We shall continue to urge the United States to provide, with the E.E.C. and other major world traders, the leadership and support which is essential if these efforts are to succeed. We had the opportunity to discuss these matters recently with members of the United States Administration when the Joint Canada-United States Committee on Trade and Economic Affairs met November 23-24 in Ottawa.

December 1, 1970
We shall have no illusions, however, that we can safely leave the protection of Canadian interests to others. As a major trading partner of Britain and a significant market for the E.E.C. and the applicant countries, Canada is not without bargaining power. These countries all wish to do more business with us; we shall insist that the terms on which we trade are fair to us as well as to them.
It will continue to be a key objective of Canadian policy to intensify our trading relations with Europe as a whole. There will be adjustments to be made because of enlargement but in view of the magnitude and variety of Europe's import needs, there should be many opportunities there for Canadian trade. We must strive to gain a share of European markets which is more in line with our role in world trade generally.
In Industry, Trade and Commerce, we have already been giving greater emphasis to this area in our departmental programs. One-third of the officer strength of our trade commissioner service is now engaged in Europe. We are devoting more resources to trade fairs and missions in the European Economic Community. We are seeking to expand the framework for scientific and technological cooperation with a number of European countries. For example, following a science and technology mission to Belgium in June, we have drafted an agreement to facilitate this type of cooperation with that country.
In the first ten months of this year, our exports to the Community were 43 per cent above those in the corresponding period of 1969. In 1970, the E.E.C. will be, for the first time, a considerably more than $1 billion market for Canadian goods.
Our activities in some of the countries which are or will be associated with the E.E.C. are also being stepped up. For example, we have just had important discussions in Ottawa with a high level delegation from Algeria. These talks have led among other things to the sale of from 850,000 to 1 million metric tons of wheat for delivery over the next four years.
We will be continually seeking ways of improving the effectiveness of our trade development activities in the E.E.C. and associated countries. I hope that Canadian exporters will also ask themselves whether there is anything more they could do to expand their sales to this dynamic trading group.
The public and private sectors in Canada will have to work closely together in order to minimize the adverse effects of E.E.C. enlargement on our trade and to maximize its positive elements. I know that we can count on all sectors of Canadian industry and I assure them that the Government will do its part.
Wednesday, December 2, 1970
